subject: business-studies
description: Business Studies question bank, FET (Amended CAPS, Grades 10-12). Keyed by atomic skill id. Each pool targets 20 items, FET pass mark 0.6, no timer. Cognitive mix per CAPS: ~30% Knowledge/Comprehension (difficulty 1), ~50% Application/Analysis (difficulty 2), ~20% Synthesis/Evaluation (difficulty 3). Tap-based mechanics only (no free-text). v1.1: Grade 10 fully authored (21 skills, 420 items).

BUS.G10.T1.MICRO.A1.title: The micro (internal) environment
BUS.G10.T1.MICRO.A1.description: Components and features of the micro environment that management controls: vision, mission, goals and objectives, organisational culture, resources and structure.
BUS.G10.T1.MICRO.A1.recovery_strategy: The micro environment is INSIDE the business and management CONTROLS it: vision, mission, goals, culture, resources, structure. If management cannot directly change it, it is not micro.

questions.question: Which environment of a business is the one that management directly controls?
questions.expected: The micro (internal) environment
questions.memo: The micro environment is inside the business — its vision, resources, culture and structure — so management controls it directly. It can only influence the market and must adapt to the macro environment.

questions.question: What does a vision statement describe?
options: What the business wants to become in the long term
What the business does day to day right now
How much profit the business made last year
The names of the business's suppliers
questions.expected: What the business wants to become in the long term
questions.memo: A vision is the long-term dream — where the business wants to be in future. The mission describes what the business does now to get there.

questions.question: True or false: A mission statement explains what the business does and who it serves in the present.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The mission is the present-tense purpose: what the business does, for whom, and how. The vision is the future aspiration.

questions.question: The shared values, beliefs and 'way things are done' inside a business is called its organisational _________.
questions.expected: culture
questions.memo: Organisational culture is the shared values and habits of the people in the business. Structure is how roles and reporting lines are arranged.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a financial resource?
options: Capital available to run the business
questions.expected: Capital available to run the business
questions.memo: Financial resources = money/capital. Physical = buildings and equipment. Human = employees and skills. Information = data the business uses.

questions.question: True or false: The number of competitors in the market is part of a business's micro environment.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Competitors belong to the market environment, which the business cannot control. The micro environment is only what is inside the business.

questions.question: Sort each item into the resource type it belongs to.

items.text: A bank loan and retained profit

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Human = people and their skills; physical = tangible things like buildings and equipment; financial = money and capital.

questions.question: Sort each statement as belonging to the micro environment or NOT belonging to it.

items.text: A new tax law passed by government
The business's own employees and resources

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Micro = inside and controllable (mission, culture, structure, resources). Tax laws and suppliers sit outside the business.

questions.question: A business writes: 'To be the most trusted bakery in the province within ten years.' What is this an example of?
questions.expected: A vision statement
questions.memo: It describes a long-term aspiration ('within ten years'), so it is a vision. A mission would say what the bakery does now.

questions.question: Why is the micro environment described as the one the business can control?
options: Because management can change its vision, structure, culture and use of resources
Because customers decide what the business does
Because the government approves every internal decision
Because competitors agree on shared rules
questions.expected: Because management can change its vision, structure, culture and use of resources
questions.memo: Control means management can directly decide and change these internal elements. It cannot decide what customers, competitors or government do.

questions.question: Goals and objectives in the micro environment are best described as _________.
options: the targets the business sets to achieve its mission
questions.expected: the targets the business sets to achieve its mission
questions.memo: Goals and objectives are internal targets that turn the mission into measurable steps. They are set and controlled by management.

questions.question: Which sequence shows the correct order from broadest direction to specific targets?
questions.expected: Vision → mission → goals → objectives
questions.memo: The vision (long-term dream) shapes the mission (what we do), which is broken into goals and then specific, measurable objectives.

questions.question: A manager wants to improve a weak organisational culture. Which action falls within her control in the micro environment?
options: Introducing shared values and recognising good teamwork
Forcing competitors to lower their prices
questions.expected: Introducing shared values and recognising good teamwork
questions.memo: Culture is internal, so a manager can shape it. Competitor prices, laws and inflation are outside the business's control.

questions.question: True or false: Organisational structure refers to how roles, authority and reporting lines are arranged inside the business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Structure is the internal arrangement of jobs and reporting lines (who reports to whom). It is part of the micro environment.

questions.question: Sort each element as a micro-environment component or a feature found OUTSIDE the business.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: If management can decide or change it, it is a micro component. Consumer tastes and exchange rates are outside forces.

questions.question: A business has a clear vision but poorly managed resources and a negative culture. Which statement best evaluates this situation?
options: A strong vision alone is not enough; the business must also manage its internal resources and culture well to succeed
The vision guarantees success regardless of the other components
Resources and culture are part of the macro environment, so they do not matter
The business should ignore culture and focus only on the vision
questions.expected: A strong vision alone is not enough; the business must also manage its internal resources and culture well to succeed
questions.memo: All micro components work together. A vision sets direction, but weak resource management and a poor culture will undermine it.

questions.question: Two businesses have identical products and prices, but one consistently outperforms the other. Which micro-environment explanation is most convincing?
options: A stronger organisational culture and better use of its resources give one business the edge
The winning business controls the macro environment
The losing business has more competitors
Customers are not part of either business
questions.expected: A stronger organisational culture and better use of its resources give one business the edge
questions.memo: When external factors (product, price) are equal, the difference lies inside — culture, management and how well resources are used.

questions.question: Build a 3-part explanation of why the micro environment is the foundation of business success.
questions.prompt: Build a 3-part explanation of why the micro environment matters most for management.

options.text: The micro environment matters because it is the one level management can directly control
The micro environment matters because the government controls it
The micro environment matters because competitors design it
Management sets the vision, shapes the culture, arranges the structure and decides how resources are used
Management decides what laws parliament passes
Management chooses how much customers earn
Because these elements are internal, the business can improve them today, while it can only adapt to the market and macro environments
Because the micro environment is the same as the macro environment
Because nothing outside the business ever affects it

questions.memo: Claim: the micro environment is controllable. Evidence: management sets vision, culture, structure, resources. Explanation: being internal, it can be changed now — unlike the market and macro levels.

questions.question: A new manager says: 'Our objectives should be specific and measurable so we can track progress.' Which micro-environment principle does this show?
options: Objectives turn the mission into clear targets the business can control and measure
Objectives are set by the business's competitors
Objectives are part of the macro environment
questions.expected: Objectives turn the mission into clear targets the business can control and measure
questions.memo: Good objectives are specific and measurable, letting management control and check progress toward the mission — an internal, controllable process.

questions.question: Sort each business action as 'controllable in the micro environment' or 'only adaptable to (outside control)'.

items.text: Responding to a rise in fuel prices
Reacting to a new competitor entering the market
Training staff to strengthen the culture

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Internal decisions (mission, structure, staff training) are controllable. Fuel prices, competitors and legislation come from the market and macro environments — the business can only adapt.

BUS.G10.T1.FUNCTIONS.A1.title: The eight business functions
BUS.G10.T1.FUNCTIONS.A1.description: Identifying and describing the eight business functions — general management, purchasing, production, marketing, public relations, human resources, administration and financing — and matching everyday tasks to the right function.
BUS.G10.T1.FUNCTIONS.A1.recovery_strategy: Tie each task to its function by its core purpose: purchasing buys stock, production makes the product, marketing sells it, HR manages people, finance handles money, admin handles information, PR manages image, general management coordinates all.

questions.question: How many business functions are there in a business?
questions.expected: Eight
questions.memo: There are eight business functions: general management, purchasing, production, marketing, public relations, human resources, administration and financing.

questions.question: True or false: The marketing function is responsible for selling the product and reaching customers.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Marketing's core job is to sell the product — advertising, promoting and reaching customers.

questions.question: The _________ function buys the stock and raw materials the business needs.
questions.expected: purchasing
questions.memo: Purchasing buys what the business needs — stock, raw materials and supplies — at the best price.

questions.question: Which function is responsible for hiring, training and managing the people who work in the business?
questions.expected: Human resources
questions.memo: Human resources (HR) manages people — hiring, training, pay and staff wellbeing.

questions.question: True or false: The production function makes or assembles the product the business sells.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Production turns raw materials into the finished product — it makes or assembles what the business sells.

questions.question: The function that handles the business's money, budgets and financial records is the _________ function.
questions.expected: financing
questions.memo: Financing (the finance function) handles money — budgets, payments, records and making sure the business can pay its bills.

questions.question: A clothing shop needs to pay its workers' wages and arrange their leave. Which function does this work?
questions.expected: Human resources
questions.memo: Anything about the people themselves — wages, leave, training — is the human resources function, even though finance pays out the money.

questions.question: A bakery phones its flour suppliers to get the best price before placing an order. Which function is doing this?
questions.expected: Purchasing
questions.memo: Getting supplies at the best price is purchasing. Production only starts once the flour arrives and is turned into bread.

questions.question: Sort each task into the business function that does it.

items.text: Ordering raw materials from a supplier
Assembling the product on the factory line
Running a social-media advert for a sale
Designing a poster to attract customers

questions.expected: All six tasks in the correct function (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Purchasing buys the inputs, production makes the product, marketing sells it. Match each task to its core purpose.

questions.question: A business pays for adverts on radio and designs a special offer to attract more buyers. Which function is responsible?
questions.expected: Marketing
questions.memo: Adverts and special offers to attract buyers are marketing. Public relations is about the business's image and reputation, not direct selling.

questions.question: After a customer complaint went viral, a company issues a public apology to protect its image. Which function handles this?
questions.expected: Public relations
questions.memo: Managing the business's image and relationship with the public and media is public relations (PR).

questions.question: True or false: The administration function handles the paperwork, filing and information the business needs to run smoothly.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Administration handles information — paperwork, filing, records and office systems — so the rest of the business can work.

questions.question: The function that coordinates all the other functions and sets the overall direction of the business is _________ management.
questions.expected: general
questions.memo: General management ties all the functions together and steers the whole business towards its goals.

questions.question: A bookkeeper records all payments received and draws up next month's budget. Which function is this?
questions.expected: Financing
questions.memo: Recording money and drawing up budgets is the financing function. Admin handles general information and paperwork, not the finances themselves.

questions.question: Sort each task into the correct business function.

items.text: Interviewing people for a new job
Keeping the office filing system up to date

questions.expected: All six tasks in the correct function (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: HR manages people, finance manages money, admin manages information and paperwork. Keep these three apart by what they look after.

questions.question: A factory takes steel and plastic and turns them into bicycles. Which function is doing this — and not the purchasing function?
options: Production turns the materials into the finished product
Purchasing turns the materials into bicycles
Marketing turns the materials into bicycles
Administration turns the materials into bicycles
questions.expected: Production turns the materials into the finished product
questions.memo: Purchasing only buys the steel and plastic; production is what turns those materials into the finished bicycles.

questions.question: Production cannot start making bread because purchasing has not bought any flour. What does this best show about the business functions?
options: The functions are interrelated and depend on each other to work
Production and purchasing are the same function
Only one function matters at a time
Purchasing should make the bread itself
questions.expected: The functions are interrelated and depend on each other to work
questions.memo: The functions are interrelated: if one (purchasing) fails, it holds up another (production). They have to work together.

questions.question: In a small spaza shop the owner does the buying, selling and bookkeeping herself, but a large supermarket has separate departments for each. Which statement best explains this?
options: The same eight functions exist in both, but a big business splits them into separate departments
Small businesses only have four functions
A big business has fewer functions than a small one
The functions only exist in large businesses
questions.expected: The same eight functions exist in both, but a big business splits them into separate departments
questions.memo: Every business has the same eight functions. In a small business one person may do several; in a big business each function becomes its own department.

questions.question: Marketing has promised customers far more stock than the shelves hold. Which combination of functions must work together to fix this?
options: Purchasing buys more materials and production makes more, guided by general management
Only marketing can solve it on its own
Public relations and administration must make the product
Human resources must manufacture the extra stock
questions.expected: Purchasing buys more materials and production makes more, guided by general management
questions.memo: A promise made by marketing needs purchasing (to buy materials) and production (to make goods), coordinated by general management — proof the functions are linked.

questions.question: Sort each task into the correct business function.

items.text: Sponsoring a local school sports day to build goodwill
Setting the business's overall goals for the year
Lowering a price to win sales from a rival
Issuing a statement to the newspapers after a recall
Deciding how the different departments will work together

questions.expected: All six tasks in the correct function (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: PR protects the image and goodwill, marketing drives sales, general management coordinates and directs the whole business. The trickiest pair is PR (reputation) versus marketing (selling).

BUS.G10.T1.MGMT.A1.title: Levels and tasks of general management
BUS.G10.T1.MGMT.A1.description: The three levels of management (top, middle, lower) and the four management tasks (planning, organising, activating/leading, controlling) — keeping the LEVEL (who) apart from the TASK (what every manager does).
BUS.G10.T1.MGMT.A1.recovery_strategy: Levels = WHO (top/middle/lower). Tasks = WHAT every manager does (plan, organise, lead, control). Top management plans long-term; lower management supervises day-to-day.

questions.question: The three levels of management are top, middle and _________.
questions.expected: lower
questions.memo: The three levels are top, middle and lower (first-line) management. 'Planning' and 'controlling' are tasks, not levels.

questions.question: True or false: Planning, organising, leading and controlling are the four management tasks.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The four tasks every manager does are planning, organising, activating/leading and controlling.

questions.question: _________ management is the highest level and is responsible for long-term planning and overall strategy.
questions.expected: Top
questions.memo: Top management (the CEO and directors) sits at the highest level and plans the long-term direction of the whole business.

questions.question: Which of these is a management TASK, not a management level?
questions.expected: Planning
questions.memo: Planning is a task every manager does. Top, middle and lower are the levels — who the managers are.

questions.question: True or false: 'Top management' is one of the three levels of management.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Top management is the highest of the three levels (top, middle, lower).

questions.question: Supervisors and foremen who oversee the day-to-day work of employees belong to _________ management.
questions.expected: lower
questions.memo: Lower (first-line) management — supervisors and foremen — runs the day-to-day work and oversees the workers directly.

questions.question: Who in a business sets the long-term goals and overall strategy?
questions.expected: Top management
questions.memo: Long-term goals and overall strategy are set by top management. Lower levels carry out and supervise the day-to-day work.

questions.question: A learner writes: 'Planning is one of the levels of management.' What is the correct way to describe planning?
options: Planning is a management task that every manager does, not a level
Planning is the top level of management
Planning is the lower level of management
questions.expected: Planning is a management task that every manager does, not a level
questions.memo: Watch the mix-up: planning is a TASK (what managers do), not a LEVEL (who they are). The levels are top, middle and lower.

questions.question: Sort each item as a level of management or a management task.
questions.expected: All six items correctly split into levels and tasks (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Levels answer WHO (top/middle/lower). Tasks answer WHAT (plan, organise, lead, control). Keep the two ideas apart.

questions.question: A supervisor checks whether workers met their daily output target and fixes any shortfalls. Which management task is this?
questions.expected: Controlling
questions.memo: Controlling means checking results against the plan and correcting problems. Checking targets and fixing shortfalls is controlling.

questions.question: Arranging the staff, money and equipment into a structure so the plan can be carried out is which management task?
questions.expected: Organising
questions.memo: Organising is arranging people and resources into a workable structure to carry out the plan.

questions.question: Which option shows the four management tasks in the order they usually happen?
questions.expected: Planning → organising → leading → controlling
questions.memo: First you plan, then you organise resources, then you lead people to do the work, and finally you control (check) the results.

questions.question: The management task of motivating, guiding and directing employees to do their work is called _________.
questions.expected: leading
questions.memo: Leading (also called activating) is motivating and guiding employees so they actually do the work that was planned.

questions.question: What is middle management's main job?
options: To turn top management's plans into action by running the departments
To set the long-term strategy for the whole business
To supervise workers on the production line minute by minute
To replace the need for top management
questions.expected: To turn top management's plans into action by running the departments
questions.memo: Middle management is the bridge: it takes top management's plans and runs the departments to make them happen, then guides lower management.

questions.question: Sort each responsibility into the management level that usually handles it.

items.text: Setting the five-year vision for the company
Coordinating a department to meet its targets
Checking that today's orders are packed

questions.expected: All six responsibilities at the correct level (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Top = long-term strategy, middle = running departments, lower = day-to-day supervision. The higher the level, the longer the time horizon.

questions.question: True or false: Lower (first-line) management is mainly responsible for the long-term strategic planning of the whole business.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Long-term strategy is top management's job. Lower management supervises the day-to-day work.

questions.question: Why does the alignment between the three management levels matter for business success?
options: If the levels do not pull in the same direction, top management's plans will not be carried out on the ground
Because only the top level does any real work
Because the levels should compete against each other
Because alignment removes the need for planning
questions.expected: If the levels do not pull in the same direction, top management's plans will not be carried out on the ground
questions.memo: The levels must align: top plans, middle organises departments, lower supervises the work. If they pull apart, good plans never reach the workers.

questions.question: A business plans and organises well and leads its staff, but never checks whether targets are being met. Which task is missing and what is the result?
options: Controlling is missing, so problems are never spotted or corrected
Planning is missing, so there are no goals
Leading is missing, so staff are not motivated
Organising is missing, so there is no structure
questions.expected: Controlling is missing, so problems are never spotted or corrected
questions.memo: Controlling closes the loop — it checks results against the plan. Without it, mistakes go unnoticed and never get fixed.

questions.question: A new manager says: 'My management level is planning.' How should this be corrected?
options: Planning is a task all managers do; her level is top, middle or lower depending on her position
She is right, planning is a management level
Planning is a business function, not a task
Her level depends on how much she plans
questions.expected: Planning is a task all managers do; her level is top, middle or lower depending on her position
questions.memo: Don't confuse the two ideas: planning is a task every level performs. Her LEVEL is decided by her position (top, middle or lower).

questions.question: Sort each activity into the management level most responsible for it.

items.text: Deciding to open branches in a new province next year
Drawing up tomorrow's staff shift roster
Making sure today's deliveries leave on time
Helping a worker fix a machine fault on the line

questions.expected: All six activities at the correct level (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Long-term, business-wide decisions sit with top management; immediate, hands-on supervision sits with lower management. The time horizon tells you the level.

BUS.G10.T1.QUALITY.A1.title: Quality and the business functions
BUS.G10.T1.QUALITY.A1.description: The concept of quality and how it applies to each business function (quality products, quality administration, a healthy financial function, quality management and a quality business image), and the link between quality and achieving objectives.
BUS.G10.T1.QUALITY.A1.recovery_strategy: Quality is everyone's job. Each function has a quality measure: production = defect-free goods, finance = accurate records, HR = skilled staff, PR = good image. Poor quality in any one drags the whole business down.

questions.question: What does 'quality' mean in a business?
options: How well a product or service meets the customer's needs and standards
How many products are made each day
questions.expected: How well a product or service meets the customer's needs and standards
questions.memo: Quality is how well something meets the needs and standards expected of it — not how cheap or how much is made.

questions.question: True or false: Quality is the job of every business function, not just production.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Quality is everyone's job. Finance, HR, admin, PR and management each have their own quality to maintain — not only production.

questions.question: Quality in the production function mainly means _________.
options: making goods with few or no faults
hiring as many workers as possible
questions.expected: making goods with few or no faults
questions.memo: Quality production means making defect-free goods that meet the standard customers expect.

questions.question: Which of these shows quality in the financial function?
questions.expected: Accurate, up-to-date financial records
questions.memo: A healthy financial function keeps accurate, reliable records so the business knows its true position.

questions.question: True or false: A good business image and reputation is a sign of quality in the public relations function.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A strong, trusted image is the PR function's quality measure — it shows the public respects the business.

questions.question: Quality in the human resources function is best shown by _________.
questions.expected: skilled, well-trained and motivated staff
questions.memo: A quality HR function produces skilled, trained and motivated staff who do their work well.

questions.question: Match each quality measure to the function it belongs to.

items.text: Goods come off the line with no defects
The books are accurate and balanced
Staff are well trained for their jobs
Products meet the agreed standard every time
Payments and budgets are handled correctly

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Each function has its own quality: production = defect-free goods, finance = accurate records, HR = skilled staff.

questions.question: A shop's products are excellent, but its records are full of mistakes and its staff are rude. What does this show about quality?
options: Quality in one function is not enough; every function must perform well
Only the product matters, so the shop is fine
Rude staff have nothing to do with quality
Record mistakes do not affect the business
questions.expected: Quality in one function is not enough; every function must perform well
questions.memo: Quality must run through every function. Great products cannot make up for poor records and poor service.

questions.question: How does good quality help a business reach its objectives?
options: It builds customer trust and repeat sales, helping the business meet its goals
It has no effect on whether goals are reached
It only increases costs with no benefit
It replaces the need for planning
questions.expected: It builds customer trust and repeat sales, helping the business meet its goals
questions.memo: Quality wins customer trust and repeat business, which helps the business achieve its sales and profit objectives.

questions.question: True or false: Poor quality in just one function can damage the whole business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Because the functions are connected, weak quality in one — like sloppy finance or rude service — drags the whole business down.

questions.question: Quality management mainly means _________.
options: managers planning, organising and checking work to keep standards high
managers spending the least money possible
managers doing all the work themselves
questions.expected: managers planning, organising and checking work to keep standards high
questions.memo: Quality management is managers leading and controlling the business so standards stay high across all functions.

questions.question: Match each example to whether it shows GOOD quality or POOR quality.

items.text: Customers get exactly what was promised
Many products are returned as faulty
The business has a trusted reputation

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Good quality means meeting standards and keeping customers happy; poor quality means faults, mistakes and ignored complaints.

questions.question: A quality administration function is one that _________.
options: keeps information accurate, organised and easy to find
makes the products on the line
questions.expected: keeps information accurate, organised and easy to find
questions.memo: Quality administration keeps records and information accurate and well organised so the business runs smoothly.

questions.question: Which statement best explains why quality is described as 'everyone's job'?
options: Every function affects the customer's experience, so each must keep its own standards high
Only the production manager can create quality
Quality is only about the price of the product
Quality is decided entirely by competitors
questions.expected: Every function affects the customer's experience, so each must keep its own standards high
questions.memo: From the product to the invoice to the service, every function touches the customer — so quality is everyone's responsibility.

questions.question: A business wants more repeat customers. Which action improves quality across functions?
options: Reduce product faults, train staff and keep accurate records
Only lower the price and change nothing else
Cut staff training to save money
questions.expected: Reduce product faults, train staff and keep accurate records
questions.memo: Improving quality everywhere — products, service and records — builds the trust that brings customers back.

questions.question: Match each quality measure to the function it belongs to.

items.text: Records that are accurate and well filed
Clear plans and good control of the business
Good media relations and community goodwill
Information that is easy to find when needed
Functions coordinated towards the same goals

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: PR = image and goodwill; administration = accurate, organised information; management = coordinating and controlling the whole business well.

questions.question: A factory makes perfect products, but its rude call centre and late deliveries are losing customers. Which evaluation is best?
options: Overall quality is poor because weak service and admin undo the good production
Quality is perfect because the products are perfect
Service and delivery are not part of quality
The factory should make even more products
questions.expected: Overall quality is poor because weak service and admin undo the good production
questions.memo: Customers judge the whole experience. Excellent products cannot make up for rude service and late delivery — overall quality is still poor.

questions.question: Two bakeries sell similar bread at the same price. One keeps clean premises, friendly service and fresh stock; it grows while the other shrinks. Which conclusion is most convincing?
options: Higher quality across the whole business helps it attract and keep customers
Quality makes no difference when prices are equal
The growing bakery must be cheating customers
Only the recipe matters, nothing else
questions.expected: Higher quality across the whole business helps it attract and keep customers
questions.memo: When price and product are equal, the bakery with better quality in service, cleanliness and freshness wins more loyal customers.

questions.question: Why is investing in quality worth the extra cost for most businesses?
options: Better quality reduces returns and complaints and builds loyal customers, helping the business meet its objectives
Quality always costs more than it is ever worth
Quality only matters to the government
questions.expected: Better quality reduces returns and complaints and builds loyal customers, helping the business meet its objectives
questions.memo: Quality cuts the cost of faults, returns and complaints, and earns loyal customers — so it usually pays for itself by helping the business reach its goals.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about quality in a business.

items.text: Every function shares responsibility for quality
Quality only concerns the production function
Good quality helps a business reach its objectives
Poor records and rude service do not affect quality
A trusted image is a sign of quality in PR
Quality means simply being the cheapest

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Quality is everyone's job, helps the business meet its goals, and is about meeting standards — not just being cheap.

BUS.G10.T1.MARKET.A1.title: The market environment
BUS.G10.T1.MARKET.A1.description: Components of the market environment (consumers, suppliers, intermediaries, competitors and other organisations), the opportunities and threats they create, and the fact that the business can influence but not control them.
BUS.G10.T1.MARKET.A1.recovery_strategy: The market environment is OUTSIDE but CLOSE: suppliers, customers, competitors, intermediaries. The business can INFLUENCE it (e.g. negotiate, advertise) but cannot CONTROL it.

questions.question: Which of these is part of the market environment?
questions.expected: The business's competitors
questions.memo: The market environment is made up of outside groups close to the business — customers, suppliers, intermediaries and competitors.

questions.question: True or false: The business can influence the market environment but cannot fully control it.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The market environment is outside the business, so it can only be influenced (through advertising, negotiation, service) — never fully controlled.

questions.question: The businesses that provide the raw materials and stock a business needs are called its _________.
questions.expected: suppliers
questions.memo: Suppliers provide the materials and stock the business buys. They are part of the market environment.

questions.question: Who are the 'consumers' in the market environment?
options: The people who buy and use the business's products
questions.expected: The people who buy and use the business's products
questions.memo: Consumers (customers) are the people who buy and use what the business sells — the heart of the market.

questions.question: True or false: Intermediaries are businesses like wholesalers and retailers that help move products from the producer to the customer.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Intermediaries (wholesalers, retailers, agents) sit between the producer and the customer and help get products to the market.

questions.question: A new shop opening nearby that sells the same goods is an example of a _________.
questions.expected: competitor
questions.memo: A competitor is another business selling similar products to the same customers. It is part of the market environment.

questions.question: Sort each group into the market-environment component it belongs to.

items.text: The wholesaler that delivers your stock
The shoppers who buy your products
A rival store selling the same goods
The farm that supplies your vegetables
The families who eat at your restaurant

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Suppliers sell TO the business, customers buy FROM it, and competitors sell the same things to the same customers.

questions.question: A supplier suddenly raises its prices. How can the business respond in the market environment?
options: Negotiate or find another supplier, because it can influence but not control suppliers
Order the supplier to lower the price
Pass a law to freeze prices
Do nothing because it controls all suppliers
questions.expected: Negotiate or find another supplier, because it can influence but not control suppliers
questions.memo: The business cannot command a supplier, but it can influence the situation — negotiate, shop around, or switch suppliers.

questions.question: Which of these is an OPPORTUNITY created by the market environment?
options: A growing number of customers wanting the product
A strong new competitor entering the area
A supplier going out of business
Customers losing interest in the product
questions.expected: A growing number of customers wanting the product
questions.memo: Opportunities are positive market changes the business can use — like growing demand. Threats are negative ones like new competitors.

questions.question: True or false: A business has direct control over what its competitors decide to do.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Competitors are outside the business. It cannot control their decisions — it can only respond and compete.

questions.question: Trade unions, NGOs and regulators are grouped in the market environment under _________.
options: other organisations the business deals with
questions.expected: other organisations the business deals with
questions.memo: Besides customers, suppliers, intermediaries and competitors, the market environment includes other organisations like unions, NGOs and regulators.

questions.question: Sort each market change as an OPPORTUNITY or a THREAT for the business.

items.text: Demand for the product is rising
A bigger competitor opens next door
A reliable new supplier offers lower prices
Customers start preferring a rival's product
A retailer agrees to stock your product

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Opportunities help the business (rising demand, better suppliers); threats put it at risk (stronger rivals, losing customers).

questions.question: How can a business INFLUENCE its customers (without controlling them)?
options: By advertising, good service and fair prices
questions.expected: By advertising, good service and fair prices
questions.memo: A business influences customers through marketing, service and pricing — it cannot force anyone to buy.

questions.question: Why is the market environment described as 'outside but close' to the business?
options: The business deals with these groups daily and can influence them, but they are not inside it
These groups are inside the business and fully controlled
These groups have no effect on the business
These groups are part of the macro economy only
questions.expected: The business deals with these groups daily and can influence them, but they are not inside it
questions.memo: The market environment is close — the business works with customers and suppliers every day — but it sits outside, so it can only be influenced.

questions.question: Sort each factor as part of the MARKET environment or part of the MICRO environment.

items.text: The business's own staff and resources
The customers who buy the product

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Micro = inside and controlled (vision, staff, structure). Market = outside but close (suppliers, competitors, customers).

questions.question: A business says: 'We will simply tell our competitors to charge higher prices.' Why will this not work?
options: Competitors are outside the business, so it cannot control their prices
Competitors always do what other businesses tell them
Competitors are part of the micro environment
There is no such thing as a competitor
questions.expected: Competitors are outside the business, so it cannot control their prices
questions.memo: A business has no authority over its competitors. It can compete with them, but it cannot tell them what to charge.

questions.question: A spaza shop notices a big supermarket is about to open nearby (threat) and that local demand for fresh bread is rising (opportunity). What is the best market-environment response?
options: Use the opportunity by selling fresh bread, while improving service to face the new competition
Ignore both changes since the shop controls the market
Try to stop the supermarket by force
questions.expected: Use the opportunity by selling fresh bread, while improving service to face the new competition
questions.memo: A smart business grabs opportunities (rising bread demand) and adapts to threats (new competitor) — it influences the market rather than trying to control it.

questions.question: Why can a business survive a difficult market environment even though it cannot control it?
options: It can influence the market through good marketing, service and supplier relationships, and adapt quickly
It can pass laws to change the market
It can order customers and competitors what to do
It does not need customers at all
questions.expected: It can influence the market through good marketing, service and supplier relationships, and adapt quickly
questions.memo: Control is not possible, but influence is — strong marketing, service and supplier ties, plus quick adapting, let a business thrive in the market.

questions.question: Two businesses face the same new competitor. One studies its customers and improves service; the other does nothing. What does this show about the market environment?
options: Businesses cannot control the market, but those that influence and adapt to it cope better
The market environment treats every business the same no matter what they do
Doing nothing is always the safest response
questions.expected: Businesses cannot control the market, but those that influence and adapt to it cope better
questions.memo: Neither business controls the competitor, but the one that influences its customers and adapts will cope far better than the one that does nothing.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about the market environment.

items.text: The business can influence but not control the market
Competitors are part of the micro environment
Suppliers, customers and competitors are all in the market environment
A business controls everything its customers do
Market changes can be opportunities or threats
Intermediaries are the workers inside the business

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: The market is outside and close: influence, not control. It holds suppliers, customers, intermediaries and competitors, and brings both opportunities and threats.

BUS.G10.T1.MACRO.A1.title: The macro environment
BUS.G10.T1.MACRO.A1.description: Components and features of the macro environment (physical/natural, economic, social/cultural/demographic, technological, legal/political, international and institutional) which the business cannot control and must adapt to.
BUS.G10.T1.MACRO.A1.recovery_strategy: The macro environment is the BIG outside world — the economy, laws, technology, society. The business has NO control and can only adapt. Market factors are specific people/firms; macro factors are broad forces.

questions.question: How much control does a business have over its macro environment?
options: No control — it can only adapt to it
Full control over all of it
questions.expected: No control — it can only adapt to it
questions.memo: The macro environment is the big outside world. A business has no control over it and can only adapt to changes like new laws or a weak economy.

questions.question: Which of these is a macro-environment factor?
options: The country's economy and interest rates
questions.expected: The country's economy and interest rates
questions.memo: The economy is a broad macro force affecting everyone. Staff and vision are micro; a single competitor is market.

questions.question: New laws and government decisions affecting business belong to the _________ component of the macro environment.
questions.expected: legal/political
questions.memo: Laws, regulations and government decisions are the legal/political part of the macro environment.

questions.question: True or false: New technology, such as faster computers and machines, is part of the macro environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Technological change is a macro force — it affects all businesses, which must adapt or fall behind.

questions.question: Droughts, floods and the climate fall under which macro-environment component?
questions.expected: Physical/natural
questions.memo: Weather, climate and natural resources are the physical/natural part of the macro environment.

questions.question: True or false: A business can pass a law to change the macro environment whenever it wants.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Only government makes laws. A business has no control over the macro environment and must adapt to it.

questions.question: Sort each factor into its macro-environment component.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Economic = money forces (inflation, interest). Technological = new machines and systems. Legal/political = laws and government rules.

questions.question: Sort each factor as part of the MARKET environment or the MACRO environment.

items.text: New technology changing the whole industry

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Market factors are specific people or firms the business deals with; macro factors are broad forces that affect everyone.

questions.question: Changes in population size, age groups and where people live form the _________ component of the macro environment.
questions.expected: social/cultural/demographic
questions.memo: Population, culture and lifestyle patterns make up the social/cultural/demographic part of the macro environment.

questions.question: Interest rates rise sharply. How should a business respond to this macro change?
options: Adapt — for example, cut borrowing and manage costs carefully
Order the bank to lower interest rates
Ignore it because it controls the economy
questions.expected: Adapt — for example, cut borrowing and manage costs carefully
questions.memo: A business cannot control interest rates. The only sensible response to a macro change is to adapt — manage costs and borrowing.

questions.question: Read the case and select the MACRO-environment factors it mentions.
questions.source_text: A small clothing factory is struggling. The rand has weakened, making imported fabric expensive. A new labour law has raised the minimum wage. Meanwhile, the factory's own machines are old and one of its regular suppliers has raised its prices.
questions.task: Tap the parts that describe macro-environment forces (broad forces the factory cannot control).

targets.reason: Exchange rates are an economic/international macro force.

targets.phrase: A new labour law has raised the minimum wage
targets.reason: Laws are a legal/political macro force.

questions.expected: The rand has weakened; A new labour law has raised the minimum wage
questions.memo: Macro forces are broad and uncontrollable: the weakening rand (economic/international) and the new labour law (legal). Old machines are micro; the supplier raising prices is a market factor.

questions.question: Why is the macro environment described as the 'big outside world'?
options: It is made of broad forces — economy, laws, technology, society — that affect all businesses
It is everything inside the business
It is only the business's suppliers
It is controlled by the business owner
questions.expected: It is made of broad forces — economy, laws, technology, society — that affect all businesses
questions.memo: The macro environment is the wide world of forces (economy, laws, technology, society) that surround and affect every business.

questions.question: True or false: A single supplier raising its prices is a macro-environment factor.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: One supplier is a specific firm, so it is a market factor. Macro factors are broad forces like inflation that affect everyone.

questions.question: Sort each factor into its macro-environment component.

items.text: More people moving to the cities
A trade agreement with another country

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Physical = nature and weather; social = people and lifestyle; international = global and cross-border forces.

questions.question: Which response shows a business correctly ADAPTING to a macro change?
options: Switching to energy-saving equipment after electricity prices rise
Telling the government to lower electricity prices
Pretending the price rise did not happen
Refusing to pay the new prices
questions.expected: Switching to energy-saving equipment after electricity prices rise
questions.memo: Adapting means changing what the business does in response to the macro force — like saving energy when prices rise.

questions.question: Read the case and select the parts that are macro-environment forces.
questions.source_text: A delivery business faces several pressures. Fuel prices have jumped because of a global oil shortage. Government has introduced a new road-safety regulation. At the same time, two of the company's drivers have resigned and a competitor has lowered its delivery fees.
questions.task: Tap the parts that describe macro-environment forces the business cannot control.

targets.phrase: Fuel prices have jumped because of a global oil shortage
targets.reason: A global price shock is an economic/international macro force.

targets.phrase: Government has introduced a new road-safety regulation
targets.reason: Regulations are a legal/political macro force.

questions.expected: Fuel prices have jumped because of a global oil shortage; Government has introduced a new road-safety regulation
questions.memo: Macro forces are broad: the global fuel shock (economic/international) and the new regulation (legal). Drivers resigning is micro; the competitor's fees are a market factor.

questions.question: During a recession (weak economy), one business cuts costs and finds cheaper local materials while another keeps spending and fails. Which conclusion is best?
options: Businesses cannot control the economy, but those that adapt to it survive better
The economy treats every business the same no matter what they do
Adapting to the macro environment makes no difference
The surviving business must control the economy
questions.expected: Businesses cannot control the economy, but those that adapt to it survive better
questions.memo: No business controls a recession, but the one that adapts — cutting costs, finding cheaper supplies — survives better than the one that does not.

questions.question: Why is it important for a business to watch the macro environment even though it cannot control it?
options: So it can see changes coming and adapt early instead of being caught by surprise
So it can pass new laws
So it can ignore its customers
questions.expected: So it can see changes coming and adapt early instead of being caught by surprise
questions.memo: Watching the macro environment lets a business prepare and adapt early to changes like new laws or a weak economy, rather than being caught off guard.

questions.question: A new technology suddenly makes a business's main product old-fashioned. Which statement best evaluates the situation?
options: The business cannot stop the technology, so it must adapt by updating its product
The business can ban the new technology
Technology is part of the micro environment, so it does not matter
The business should keep making the old product unchanged forever
questions.expected: The business cannot stop the technology, so it must adapt by updating its product
questions.memo: Technological change is an uncontrollable macro force. The business must adapt — update or replace its product — to stay relevant.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about the macro environment.

items.text: The business must adapt to the macro environment
The business controls the macro environment
Laws, the economy and technology are macro forces
One nearby competitor is a macro factor
Macro factors are broad and affect all businesses
A business can pass its own laws

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: The macro environment is broad and uncontrollable — economy, laws, technology, society — and the business can only adapt. Single firms are market factors, not macro.

BUS.G10.T1.INTERREL.A1.title: How the three environments interrelate
BUS.G10.T1.INTERREL.A1.description: The relationship between the micro, market and macro environments, the degree of control over each (control, influence, no control), and how a change in one environment ripples into the others.
BUS.G10.T1.INTERREL.A1.recovery_strategy: Control decreases as you move outward: micro (control) → market (influence) → macro (no control). The three are connected: a macro change (e.g. a new law) forces the business to change its micro decisions.

questions.question: Which environment does the business have FULL control over?
questions.expected: The micro environment
questions.memo: Control decreases as you move outward: full control over the micro (inside), influence over the market, no control over the macro.

questions.question: The business can INFLUENCE but not control which environment?
questions.expected: The market environment
questions.memo: The market environment (suppliers, customers, competitors) can be influenced through marketing and negotiation, but not fully controlled.

questions.question: As you move from the micro to the macro environment, the business's control _________.
questions.expected: decreases
questions.memo: Control decreases outward: full control (micro), some influence (market), no control (macro).

questions.question: True or false: A change in the macro environment can affect the micro environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The three environments are connected. A macro change like a new law forces the business to change its internal (micro) decisions.

questions.question: True or false: The three environments are completely separate and never affect each other.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: The environments are interrelated — a change in one ripples into the others. They are not separate.

questions.question: Over which environment does the business have NO control?
questions.expected: The macro environment
questions.memo: The macro environment (economy, laws, technology) is beyond the business's control — it can only adapt.

questions.question: Match each environment to the level of control the business has over it.

items.text: The business's own structure and culture

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Micro = full control, market = influence, macro = no control. The same pattern applies to the examples in each.

questions.question: Government raises the minimum wage (macro). How does this ripple into the micro environment?
options: The business must change its internal budgets and staffing decisions
Nothing inside the business changes at all
The business can cancel the law
questions.expected: The business must change its internal budgets and staffing decisions
questions.memo: A macro change (new wage law) ripples inward: the business must adjust its own budgets and staffing — its micro decisions.

questions.question: Which example shows a market change rippling into the micro environment?
options: A new competitor forces the business to retrain its staff and improve its products
Inflation is caused by the business
The business writes the country's laws
questions.expected: A new competitor forces the business to retrain its staff and improve its products
questions.memo: A market change (new competitor) pushes the business to change inside — retraining staff, improving products — showing how the environments connect.

questions.question: The business has the MOST control over the environment that is _________.
options: closest to it — the internal micro environment
furthest from it — the macro environment
questions.expected: closest to it — the internal micro environment
questions.memo: Control is strongest where the business is closest in — the internal micro environment — and weakest far out in the macro world.

questions.question: Read both views, then decide which source each statement matches.

source_a.text: Our business plans only around what happens inside our walls. The economy and new laws are someone else's problem — we just focus on our own staff and products.

source_b.text: We watch interest rates, new laws and technology closely. When the outside world changes, we change our internal plans to match it.

statements.text: Treats the three environments as connected
Runs a business with a micro environment
Claims to control the national economy

questions.expected: s1=b_only, s2=a_only, s3=both, s4=neither
questions.memo: Business B sees the environments as connected and adapts; Business A wrongly treats them as separate. Both have a micro environment, and neither controls the economy.

questions.question: Why is it a mistake to plan a business as if the three environments are separate?
options: Because a change in one environment usually affects the others, so they must be planned together
Because only the macro environment matters
Because the business controls all three equally
questions.expected: Because a change in one environment usually affects the others, so they must be planned together
questions.memo: The environments are interrelated. Planning them separately ignores how a change in one ripples into the others.

questions.question: True or false: The business can respond to a macro change by adjusting things in its micro environment.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Although it cannot control the macro environment, the business can react by changing its own micro decisions — budgets, products, staffing.

questions.question: Sort each action by the environment it takes place in.

items.text: Negotiating a deal with a supplier
Adjusting to a new national tax law

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Inside actions = micro (control); dealing with suppliers/customers = market (influence); coping with laws and the economy = macro (adapt).

questions.question: A bank raises interest rates (macro). Trace the most likely ripple.
options: Borrowing becomes costly (market), so the business cuts spending and delays hiring (micro)
The business changes the interest rate back (macro)
questions.expected: Borrowing becomes costly (market), so the business cuts spending and delays hiring (micro)
questions.memo: A macro change ripples through the market (costly borrowing) into the micro environment (cutting spending, delaying hiring) — showing how connected they are.

questions.question: Which statement correctly summarises the control over the three environments?
options: Control over micro, influence over market, no control over macro
No control over micro, full control over macro
Equal full control over all three
Influence over micro, control over macro
questions.expected: Control over micro, influence over market, no control over macro
questions.memo: The rule is simple: control (micro) → influence (market) → no control (macro), decreasing as you move outward.

questions.question: A new technology (macro) appears. A business updates its products (micro) and renegotiates with suppliers (market). Which conclusion is best?
options: A single macro change can force changes across all three environments, because they are interrelated
The three environments worked separately here
The business controlled the new technology
Only the macro environment was affected
questions.expected: A single macro change can force changes across all three environments, because they are interrelated
questions.memo: One macro change pushed the business to act in its micro and market environments too — clear proof the three are interrelated.

questions.question: Why does understanding the interrelationship help a business manage risk?
options: It can prepare its internal plans early when it sees a market or macro change coming
It can stop all outside changes from happening
It can ignore the macro environment safely
It can control its competitors and the economy
questions.expected: It can prepare its internal plans early when it sees a market or macro change coming
questions.memo: Because the environments are connected, spotting an outside change early lets a business adjust its internal plans before the risk hits hard.

questions.question: Two shops face the same new law (macro). Shop A changes its prices and stock (micro) and talks to suppliers (market); Shop B does nothing. What does this show?
options: Because the environments are connected, the shop that adjusts across all three copes better
questions.expected: Because the environments are connected, the shop that adjusts across all three copes better
questions.memo: The law ripples through all three environments. The shop that responds across its micro and market environments copes far better than the one that ignores the link.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about how the environments interrelate.

items.text: Control decreases from micro to macro
The three environments never affect each other
A macro change can force micro changes
The business fully controls the macro environment
The business can only influence the market environment
The micro environment is the hardest to control

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Control runs control → influence → no control from micro to macro, and the three are connected so changes ripple between them.

BUS.G10.T1.SECTORS.A1.title: Business sectors
BUS.G10.T1.SECTORS.A1.description: Classifying industries into primary, secondary and tertiary sectors; the difference between the formal and informal sectors; and the difference between the public and private sectors.
BUS.G10.T1.SECTORS.A1.recovery_strategy: Primary = extract raw materials (mining, farming). Secondary = make/process them (factories). Tertiary = services (shops, banks, transport). Formal vs informal = registered & taxed vs not. Public vs private = government-owned vs privately owned.

questions.question: Which sector takes raw materials straight from nature, like mining and farming?
questions.expected: The primary sector
questions.memo: The primary sector extracts raw materials from nature — mining, farming, fishing and forestry.

questions.question: The sector that turns raw materials into finished goods in factories is the _________ sector.
questions.expected: secondary
questions.memo: The secondary sector processes or manufactures raw materials into products — for example a factory making bread from flour.

questions.question: Shops, banks and transport companies belong to which sector?
questions.expected: The tertiary sector
questions.memo: The tertiary sector provides services — selling, banking, transport, tourism — rather than making goods.

questions.question: True or false: A business that is registered and pays tax is part of the formal sector.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The formal sector is made up of registered businesses that pay tax and follow the law. The informal sector is not registered.

questions.question: A business owned and run by the government is part of the _________ sector.
questions.expected: public
questions.memo: The public sector is owned by government (e.g. Eskom, a public hospital). The private sector is owned by private people or companies.

questions.question: True or false: A street vendor selling fruit without being registered is in the informal sector.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: The informal sector is unregistered and untaxed, like a street vendor or a spaza shop that is not registered.

questions.question: Sort each business into its sector.

items.text: A bakery turning flour into bread

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Primary takes from nature (mine, farm); secondary makes/processes (factory, bakery); tertiary serves (shop, bank).

questions.question: Why is a bakery placed in the SECONDARY sector, not the primary sector?
options: It processes a raw material (flour) into a finished product (bread)
It digs the wheat out of the ground
It only sells, never makes anything
It is owned by the government
questions.expected: It processes a raw material (flour) into a finished product (bread)
questions.memo: A bakery changes flour into bread — that is processing, which is the secondary sector. The primary sector only extracts the raw material.

questions.question: Sort each business as FORMAL or INFORMAL sector.

items.text: A registered company that pays tax
A backyard mechanic with no registration

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Formal = registered and taxed, following the law; informal = not registered and not taxed.

questions.question: Which of these is a PUBLIC-sector organisation?
questions.expected: A government-run public hospital
questions.memo: The public sector is owned by government — like a public hospital. Privately owned businesses are in the private sector.

questions.question: A fishing boat catches fish, a cannery tins them, and a shop sells the tins. In order, the sectors are _________.
questions.expected: primary, secondary, tertiary
questions.memo: Catching fish = primary (from nature); canning = secondary (processing); selling = tertiary (service). Goods often pass through all three.

questions.question: True or false: A bakery that bakes and sells bread is in the primary sector.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: Baking changes flour into bread — that is processing, so a bakery is secondary, not primary. Primary only extracts raw materials.

questions.question: What is the main difference between the public and private sectors?
options: The public sector is owned by government; the private sector is owned by private people
The public sector never charges money; the private sector always does
The public sector only mines; the private sector only farms
questions.expected: The public sector is owned by government; the private sector is owned by private people
questions.memo: Ownership is the key: public = government-owned; private = owned by private individuals or companies.

questions.question: Sort each business as PUBLIC or PRIVATE sector.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: If government owns it, it is public; if private people or companies own it, it is private.

questions.question: Why does the informal sector still matter to the economy even though it pays no tax?
options: It creates jobs and income for many people who cannot find formal work
It pays the most tax of all sectors
It is owned by the government
questions.expected: It creates jobs and income for many people who cannot find formal work
questions.memo: The informal sector provides income and jobs for many South Africans, even though it is unregistered and untaxed.

questions.question: A registered tour company that drives tourists around is in which sector(s)?
options: The tertiary sector and the formal sector
questions.expected: The tertiary sector and the formal sector
questions.memo: Providing a service = tertiary; being registered and taxed = formal. A business can be described by more than one classification at once.

questions.question: A learner says: 'A diamond mine and a jewellery factory are both primary, because both deal with diamonds.' Which evaluation is correct?
options: No — the mine is primary (extracting), but the factory is secondary (processing the diamonds)
questions.expected: No — the mine is primary (extracting), but the factory is secondary (processing the diamonds)
questions.memo: Dealing with the same material does not mean the same sector. Extracting = primary (mine); processing into jewellery = secondary (factory).

questions.question: Why does a developed economy usually have a large tertiary sector?
options: As economies grow, more people need and can afford services like banking, retail and transport
Developed economies stop making and growing things entirely
Services are the only legal businesses
questions.expected: As economies grow, more people need and can afford services like banking, retail and transport
questions.memo: As an economy develops, demand for services (the tertiary sector) grows — banking, retail, transport, tourism — so that sector becomes large.

questions.question: A spaza shop is unregistered and owned by one person. How is it best classified?
questions.expected: Tertiary, informal and private sector
questions.memo: It sells goods (tertiary service), is unregistered (informal) and is privately owned (private) — three classifications describing the same business.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about business sectors.

items.text: Mining and farming are primary-sector activities
A factory making goods is in the primary sector
The formal sector is registered and pays tax
The public sector is owned by private people
Shops and banks are tertiary-sector businesses
An unregistered street trader is in the formal sector

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Primary = extract, secondary = make, tertiary = serve; formal = registered/taxed; public = government-owned. Each statement tests one of these rules.

BUS.G10.T2.SOCIOECON.A1.title: Contemporary socio-economic issues
BUS.G10.T2.SOCIOECON.A1.description: Identifying contemporary socio-economic issues that affect business — unemployment, poverty, HIV/Aids, crime, strikes, piracy, counterfeiting, gambling, violence, inclusivity and the skills levy — and connecting each issue to its concrete impact on a business.
BUS.G10.T2.SOCIOECON.A1.strand: T2 — Socio-economic issues, social responsibility, entrepreneurship & ownership
BUS.G10.T2.SOCIOECON.A1.recovery_strategy: Every socio-economic issue hits business through cost or productivity: crime raises security costs, HIV/Aids reduces the labour force, strikes stop production, piracy steals sales.

questions.question: What does unemployment mean?
options: People who want to work cannot find jobs
questions.expected: People who want to work cannot find jobs
questions.memo: Unemployment is when people who are able and willing to work cannot find jobs.

questions.question: True or false: Crime increases the security costs a business has to pay.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Crime forces businesses to spend more on guards, alarms and fencing — a direct extra cost.

questions.question: When workers stop work to demand better pay or conditions, this is called a _________.
questions.expected: strike
questions.memo: A strike is when workers stop working to push for better pay or conditions, which halts production.

questions.question: What is piracy in a business sense?
options: Illegally copying someone else's product, music or design
questions.expected: Illegally copying someone else's product, music or design
questions.memo: Piracy is illegally copying protected work — breaking copyright, patent or trademark rules — and selling it.

questions.question: True or false: HIV/Aids can reduce the number of workers a business has available.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: HIV/Aids can make workers ill or absent, reducing the available workforce and lowering output.

questions.question: Selling fake branded goods as if they were the real thing is called _________.
questions.expected: counterfeiting
questions.memo: Counterfeiting is making and selling fake copies of branded goods, which steals sales from the real business.

questions.question: How does a high crime rate most directly affect a business?
options: It raises costs through stock losses and extra spending on security
It has no effect on the business at all
questions.expected: It raises costs through stock losses and extra spending on security
questions.memo: Crime hits the business through cost: stolen stock and money spent on guards, cameras and fencing.

questions.question: How does a long strike affect a business?
options: Production stops, so output falls and orders are late
Production speeds up and profits rise
questions.expected: Production stops, so output falls and orders are late
questions.memo: A strike stops work, so the business produces less and may miss orders — an impact on productivity.

questions.question: Match each business effect to the socio-economic issue that causes it.

items.text: More money spent on guards and alarms
Sales lost to illegal copies of the product
Goods not made, so orders are late
The brand's design is copied without permission

questions.expected: All six effects matched to the correct issue (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Crime raises costs and losses, strikes stop production, piracy and counterfeiting steal sales and copy the brand.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the skills levy that businesses pay?
options: To raise money to fund the training and skilling of workers
questions.expected: To raise money to fund the training and skilling of workers
questions.memo: The skills levy is money businesses pay to help fund worker training and address the shortage of skills.

questions.question: Read the passage and highlight the socio-economic issues affecting the factory.
questions.source_text: A factory struggled this year. A long strike stopped production for three weeks. Rising crime forced the owner to spend more on security. The factory had also bought a new delivery van. Cheaper counterfeit copies of its products appeared in local markets.
questions.task: Highlight the socio-economic issues affecting the factory, and leave normal business activities unmarked.

targets.phrase: A long strike stopped production for three weeks
Rising crime forced the owner to spend more on security
Cheaper counterfeit copies of its products appeared in local markets

questions.expected: Highlight the strike, the crime and the counterfeiting (≥2 correct, ≤1 wrong)
questions.memo: The strike, crime and counterfeiting are socio-economic issues. Buying a delivery van is a normal business activity, so leave it unmarked.

questions.question: _________ means including everyone fairly, regardless of race, gender or disability.
questions.expected: Inclusivity
questions.memo: Inclusivity is making sure everyone is fairly included and treated equally, whatever their background.

questions.question: How does counterfeiting most affect a well-known brand?
options: It loses sales and its reputation is damaged by poor-quality fakes
It gains free advertising and higher profit
It has no effect on the brand
questions.expected: It loses sales and its reputation is damaged by poor-quality fakes
questions.memo: Fakes take sales away and, when they are poor quality, damage the trust customers have in the real brand.

questions.question: Sort each item as a socio-economic issue or a normal business activity.

items.text: Painting the shop a new colour

questions.expected: All six items correctly sorted (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Socio-economic issues are wider social and economic problems (unemployment, poverty, crime, HIV/Aids). Buying chairs or painting a shop is just everyday business.

questions.question: How can high levels of gambling and violence in a community affect a business's workers?
options: They can lower workers' focus and productivity and increase absenteeism
They have no link to the workplace
questions.expected: They can lower workers' focus and productivity and increase absenteeism
questions.memo: Social problems like gambling and violence can distract workers, cause stress and absences, and lower productivity.

questions.question: True or false: Widespread poverty reduces the number of customers who can afford a business's products.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: When people are poor they have less money to spend, so the business has fewer paying customers and lower sales.

questions.question: Read the passage and highlight the parts that show the business IMPACT of the riots.
questions.source_text: When riots hit the town, the shop felt it in many ways. Stock was looted from the shelves. Customers stayed home, so daily sales dropped sharply. The shop had to pay overtime to clean up and reopen. Its insurance later covered part of the damage.
questions.task: Highlight the parts that describe how the riots actually hurt the business.

targets.phrase: Stock was looted from the shelves
pay overtime to clean up and reopen
