questions.expected: Highlight the looted stock, the dropped sales and the overtime cost (≥2 correct, ≤1 wrong)
questions.memo: The impacts are the looted stock, the drop in sales and the overtime cost. The insurance covering part of the damage softens the blow — it is not itself a harm, so leave it unmarked.

questions.question: Why should a business care about socio-economic issues even when it did not cause them?
options: Because these issues still affect its costs, workers and customers
Because the issues never reach the business
Because caring lowers its tax automatically
Because only government is affected by them
questions.expected: Because these issues still affect its costs, workers and customers
questions.memo: Whether or not it caused them, these issues reach the business through higher costs, sick or distracted workers and poorer customers, so it must respond.

questions.question: In a town with high unemployment and deep poverty, a shop's sales keep falling. Which explanation best links the issues to the business?
options: Fewer people have jobs and money, so fewer can afford to buy, lowering sales
Unemployment makes people spend much more
Poverty has nothing to do with shop sales
The shop's sales fall only because of its own prices
questions.expected: Fewer people have jobs and money, so fewer can afford to buy, lowering sales
questions.memo: Unemployment and poverty mean less money in the community, fewer paying customers and falling sales — a clear chain from issue to business impact.

questions.question: Sort each impact by how the socio-economic issue mainly hits the business.

items.text: Workers off sick, so less is made
A strike halting the production line

questions.expected: All six impacts sorted by how they hit the business (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Issues hit business three ways: raising costs (security, insurance), lowering productivity (illness, strikes) or reducing sales (poverty, counterfeits).

BUS.G10.T2.SOCRESP.A1.title: Social responsibility & CSR
BUS.G10.T2.SOCRESP.A1.description: What social responsibility means, the definition of Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR), and how a business voluntarily gives back to its community — kept apart from simply obeying the law.
BUS.G10.T2.SOCRESP.A1.strand: T2 — Socio-economic issues, social responsibility, entrepreneurship & ownership
BUS.G10.T2.SOCRESP.A1.recovery_strategy: Social responsibility = a business voluntarily giving back to society and the environment, beyond what the law requires. CSR = the company-wide programme that does this (e.g. funding a school, cleaning a river).

questions.question: What does social responsibility mean for a business?
options: Voluntarily giving back to society and the environment, beyond what the law requires
Only paying the taxes the law demands
Making the highest possible profit and nothing else
Following safety rules because it is forced to
questions.expected: Voluntarily giving back to society and the environment, beyond what the law requires
questions.memo: Social responsibility is voluntary — doing good for society and the environment over and above what the law already requires.

questions.question: True or false: CSR stands for Corporate Social Responsibility.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: CSR = Corporate Social Responsibility — the company-wide programme through which a business gives back.

questions.question: Social responsibility means doing good that goes _________ what the law requires.
questions.expected: beyond
questions.memo: The key idea is 'beyond': social responsibility is what the business chooses to do over and above its legal duties.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of CSR?
options: Paying its workers the minimum wage
questions.expected: Funding a local school's library
questions.memo: Funding a school is a voluntary gift to the community — CSR. The others are legal duties the business must do anyway.

questions.question: True or false: Paying tax is an example of CSR.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — paying tax is a legal duty, not CSR. CSR is what the business chooses to do voluntarily, beyond the law.

questions.question: CSR is the company-wide _________ through which a business gives back to its community.
questions.expected: programme
questions.memo: CSR is the organised, company-wide programme that delivers a business's social responsibility.

questions.question: Which of these is CSR, rather than a legal obligation?
options: Sponsoring meals at a local soup kitchen
Keeping the workplace safe as the law requires
questions.expected: Sponsoring meals at a local soup kitchen
questions.memo: Sponsoring a soup kitchen is a voluntary good deed — CSR. Paying UIF, registering and safety are legal must-dos.

questions.question: A factory chooses to plant trees and clean the river near its site, even though no law requires it. Is this CSR?
options: Yes — it is voluntarily giving back to the environment
No — protecting the environment can never be CSR
No — it is only CSR if the law demands it
Yes — but only because it saves the factory money
questions.expected: Yes — it is voluntarily giving back to the environment
questions.memo: Choosing to help the environment when no law forces it is exactly CSR — voluntary giving back.

questions.question: Thesis: 'A business should give back to its community through social responsibility.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: A business should give back to its community through social responsibility.

pool.text: It builds the business's reputation and earns customer trust
It helps solve real local problems like poverty and unemployment
It attracts and keeps good staff who are proud of the company
Giving anything away always bankrupts a business
The owner likes the colour of the company logo
It is only worth doing when the law forces it

questions.memo: The strong reasons are reputation, solving real community problems and attracting proud staff. The others are a counter-claim, an irrelevant point and a weak claim that misses the voluntary nature of CSR.

questions.question: Build an explanation of why social responsibility matters to a business.
questions.prompt: Pick the best option for each slot to explain why social responsibility matters.

options.text: A business should voluntarily give back to the society it depends on
A business should give back only when the law forces it to
A business should never spend money on its community
Funding schools, clinics and clean-ups helps the community the business operates in
Paying its normal taxes is the only thing a business can ever do
Ignoring the community has no effect on the business
A stronger, healthier community gives the business better workers and loyal customers
Communities have nothing to do with a business's success
Giving back is exactly the same as obeying the law

questions.memo: Claim: a business should voluntarily give back. Evidence: funding schools, clinics and clean-ups. Explanation: a healthier community gives the business better workers and loyal customers.

questions.question: What is the key difference between CSR and simply obeying the law?
options: CSR is voluntary and goes beyond the law; obeying the law is compulsory
CSR and obeying the law are exactly the same
CSR is forced, while obeying the law is a choice
CSR only applies to government departments
questions.expected: CSR is voluntary and goes beyond the law; obeying the law is compulsory
questions.memo: Obeying the law is compulsory; CSR is the voluntary extra a business chooses to do for society.

questions.question: Giving back to its _________ community — the area around it — is a key part of a business's CSR.
questions.expected: immediate
questions.memo: CSR usually starts with the immediate community — the people and area closest to where the business operates.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT an example of CSR?
options: Paying the company's income tax to SARS
Running a free skills workshop for the community
questions.expected: Paying the company's income tax to SARS
questions.memo: Paying tax is a legal obligation, not CSR. Bursaries, donations and free workshops are voluntary giving back.

questions.question: True or false: CSR can improve a business's image and reputation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: When a business is seen helping its community, customers trust and respect it more — improving its image.

questions.question: A company sets up bursaries to train unemployed young people in the area. Which socio-economic issue is its CSR addressing?
options: Unemployment and a shortage of skills
questions.expected: Unemployment and a shortage of skills
questions.memo: Bursaries that train young people directly tackle unemployment and the skills shortage — a clear CSR initiative aimed at a real issue.

questions.question: Why is CSR described as voluntary rather than forced?
options: Because the business chooses to do it, beyond what the law makes it do
Because the government pays for all of it
Because the law punishes businesses that skip it
Because customers vote on every donation
questions.expected: Because the business chooses to do it, beyond what the law makes it do
questions.memo: CSR is voluntary: the business decides to give back on its own, over and above its legal duties.

questions.question: Thesis: 'Spending money on CSR is good for a business in the long run.' Choose the THREE strongest reasons.
questions.thesis: Spending money on CSR is good for a business in the long run.

pool.text: A trusted, respected brand attracts loyal customers over time
Healthier, better-educated communities become better customers and workers
Good CSR gives the business an edge over rivals who do nothing
That money could simply have gone to bigger manager bonuses
The CEO happens to drive an expensive car
CSR only matters during the festive season

questions.memo: Long-term gains come from brand trust, stronger communities and an edge over rivals. The bonus point is a counter, the CEO's car is irrelevant, and 'only at festive season' is a weak claim.

questions.question: Build a balanced explanation of whether CSR is worth its cost.
questions.prompt: Pick the best option for each slot to weigh up whether CSR is worth the cost.

options.text: CSR costs money now but builds long-term value for the business
CSR is a pure waste with no benefit at all
CSR is legally compulsory for every business
A good reputation from CSR brings loyal customers and proud staff
CSR has no effect on customers or staff
CSR removes the need to make any profit
The reputation and goodwill gained usually outweigh the money spent over time
The money spent can never bring anything back
CSR only counts if the government pays for it

questions.memo: Claim: CSR costs now but builds long-term value. Evidence: reputation brings loyal customers and proud staff. Explanation: the goodwill usually outweighs the spend over time.

questions.question: A business owner says: 'Paying my workers on time is my CSR.' How should this be corrected?
options: Paying wages on time is a legal duty; CSR is the voluntary extra she does for the community
She is right, paying wages is CSR
CSR means she does not have to pay wages
Paying wages late would be better CSR
questions.expected: Paying wages on time is a legal duty; CSR is the voluntary extra she does for the community
questions.memo: Don't confuse the two: paying wages on time is required by law. CSR is the voluntary good she chooses to do beyond that.

questions.question: Which statement best explains how CSR can support a business's long-term success?
options: By building goodwill and stronger communities, CSR creates loyal customers and a better workforce over time
CSR guarantees instant profit the same week it is done
CSR has no link to a business's future
CSR only helps the community and never the business
questions.expected: By building goodwill and stronger communities, CSR creates loyal customers and a better workforce over time
questions.memo: CSR is a long-term investment: goodwill and healthier communities give the business loyal customers and better workers down the line.

BUS.G10.T2.ENTRE.A1.title: Entrepreneurial qualities
BUS.G10.T2.ENTRE.A1.description: Identifying the personal qualities of an entrepreneur — risk-taking, perseverance, confidence, passion, a clear vision, adaptability, leadership, commitment and organisational skills — and keeping these qualities apart from business resources.
BUS.G10.T2.ENTRE.A1.strand: T2 — Socio-economic issues, social responsibility, entrepreneurship & ownership
BUS.G10.T2.ENTRE.A1.recovery_strategy: Entrepreneurial qualities are personal characteristics, not resources: how the person thinks and behaves (risk-taking, perseverance, vision) — not what they own.

questions.question: Which of these is an entrepreneurial quality?
questions.expected: Risk-taking
questions.memo: Risk-taking is a personal quality — how the entrepreneur behaves. A factory, loan or truck are resources the business owns.

questions.question: True or false: Perseverance — not giving up — is an entrepreneurial quality.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Perseverance, the drive to keep going through setbacks, is a key entrepreneurial quality.

questions.question: An entrepreneur who keeps trying again after several failures is showing _________.
questions.expected: perseverance
questions.memo: Trying again after failure is perseverance — a personal quality, not something the person owns.

questions.question: Which of these is a business resource, NOT an entrepreneurial quality?
questions.expected: Money in the bank
questions.memo: Money is a resource the business has. Confidence, vision and determination are personal qualities of the entrepreneur.

questions.question: True or false: Having a clear vision for the future is an entrepreneurial quality.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A clear vision — knowing where you want the business to go — is an important entrepreneurial quality.

questions.question: Being willing to take a chance on a new idea, even when the outcome is uncertain, is called _________.
questions.expected: risk-taking
questions.memo: Risk-taking is the willingness to back a new idea despite uncertainty — a core entrepreneurial quality.

questions.question: An entrepreneur walks into a tough meeting with investors, sure of her idea and able to answer every doubt. Which quality is she showing?
questions.expected: Confidence
questions.memo: Believing in her idea and handling doubts shows confidence — a personal quality, not a resource.

questions.question: When the market suddenly changes, an entrepreneur quickly adjusts her product and plans. Which quality is this?
questions.expected: Flexibility (adaptability)
questions.memo: Adjusting quickly to change is flexibility or adaptability — the ability to change plans when circumstances change.

questions.question: Sort each item as an entrepreneurial quality or a business resource.

items.text: A clear vision for the future

questions.expected: All six items split into qualities and resources (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Qualities are personal characteristics (how the person thinks and behaves). Resources are things the business owns (money, vehicles, buildings).

questions.question: An entrepreneur loves what she does and works long hours because she truly believes in her business. Which quality is this?
questions.expected: Passion
questions.memo: Deep belief and love for the work is passion — the energy that drives an entrepreneur on.

questions.question: Thesis: 'An entrepreneur needs the right personal qualities, not just money, to succeed.' Choose the THREE strongest supporting reasons.
questions.thesis: An entrepreneur needs the right personal qualities, not just money, to succeed.

pool.text: Perseverance keeps the entrepreneur going through hard times
A clear vision guides every decision the business makes
Willingness to take calculated risks lets the business grow
All you really need is a big bank balance
The entrepreneur owns a nice car
Qualities only matter on weekends

questions.memo: Perseverance, vision and risk-taking are real qualities that drive success. 'Just a bank balance' is a counter-claim, the car is irrelevant, and 'only on weekends' is weak.

questions.question: The ability to change plans when circumstances change is the quality of _________.
questions.expected: adaptability
questions.memo: Adaptability (flexibility) is being able to change plans as the situation changes — vital for an entrepreneur.

questions.question: Which scenario shows perseverance rather than risk-taking?
options: Reopening the business after the first attempt failed
Investing savings in a brand-new, untested idea
questions.expected: Reopening the business after the first attempt failed
questions.memo: Perseverance is pushing on after failure. Backing an untested idea or expanding quickly is risk-taking.

questions.question: Match each scenario to the entrepreneurial quality it best shows.

items.text: Investing savings in an untested idea
Trying again after the first shop failed
Motivating the team to reach a goal
Launching a product before rivals despite uncertainty
Working through tough months without giving up
Guiding and inspiring staff through change

questions.expected: All six scenarios matched to the right quality (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Risk-taking = backing an uncertain idea; perseverance = not giving up; leadership = guiding and motivating people.

questions.question: True or false: Having lots of money is an entrepreneurial quality.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — money is a resource, not a quality. Qualities describe how the entrepreneur thinks and behaves, not what they own.

questions.question: An entrepreneur plans her week carefully, keeps neat records and never misses a deadline. Which quality is this?
questions.expected: Organisational skills
questions.memo: Planning, ordering tasks and meeting deadlines shows organisational skills — a personal quality.

questions.question: Thesis: 'Personal qualities matter more than starting money for a new entrepreneur.' Choose the THREE strongest reasons.
questions.thesis: Personal qualities matter more than starting money for a new entrepreneur.

pool.text: A determined person can attract investors and resources over time
Adaptability lets the entrepreneur survive when the market changes
Passion and energy keep the business going when money is tight
Without any money at all a business can never even start
The entrepreneur's favourite colour is blue
Qualities are only useful for big companies

questions.memo: Determination attracts resources, adaptability survives change, and passion sustains the business when cash is short. The 'no money, no start' point is a fair counter, the colour is irrelevant, and 'only big companies' is weak.

questions.question: One person has start-up money but gives up at the first problem; another has little money but great perseverance and vision. Who is more likely to build a lasting business, and why?
options: The second, because qualities like perseverance and vision drive long-term success
The first, because money alone guarantees success
Neither, because qualities and money are irrelevant
The first, because perseverance is a resource
questions.expected: The second, because qualities like perseverance and vision drive long-term success
questions.memo: Money runs out or gets wasted without the right person behind it. Perseverance and vision keep a business going and help it find the resources it needs.

questions.question: Why are entrepreneurial qualities often said to matter more than resources at the start of a business?
options: A person with strong qualities can attract and make good use of resources, but resources alone do nothing
Resources can think and plan on their own
Qualities cost more than resources to buy
Resources always run a business by themselves
questions.expected: A person with strong qualities can attract and make good use of resources, but resources alone do nothing
questions.memo: Resources are useless without a capable person. Strong qualities let an entrepreneur attract investors and use resources well.

questions.question: Sort each item as an entrepreneurial quality or a business resource. Watch the tricky ones.
questions.expected: All six items split into qualities and resources (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Confidence, adaptability and drive are personal qualities. A loan, equipment and stock are resources the business owns. Keep the two ideas apart.

BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A1.title: Forms of ownership: sole trader & partnership
BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A1.description: The characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of the sole proprietor and the partnership and the differences between them — capital, liability, continuity, taxation and the division of profits. Both have unlimited liability and no separate legal identity.
BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A1.strand: T2 — Socio-economic issues, social responsibility, entrepreneurship & ownership
BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A1.recovery_strategy: Sole trader and partnership both have UNLIMITED liability (owners are personally liable for debts) and no separate legal identity. Partnerships add more capital and shared skills but also shared liability.

questions.question: A sole trader (sole proprietor) is a business owned by:
questions.expected: One person
questions.memo: A sole trader is owned and run by one person, who makes all decisions and keeps all the profit.

questions.question: True or false: A partnership is owned by two or more people.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A partnership is owned by two or more partners who share the capital, work, profits and responsibility.

questions.question: A sole trader has _________ liability, which means personal belongings can be used to pay business debts.
questions.expected: unlimited
questions.memo: A sole trader has unlimited liability: there is no line between the owner and the business, so personal assets can be taken for business debts.

questions.question: Which of these is an advantage of being a sole trader?
options: The owner keeps all the profit and has full control
The business is a separate legal person
Profits must be shared with partners
questions.expected: The owner keeps all the profit and has full control
questions.memo: A sole trader keeps all profit and controls every decision — a key advantage. (Limited liability and separate legal identity do NOT apply.)

questions.question: True or false: A sole trader's personal belongings can be taken to pay the business's debts.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: True — because of unlimited liability, the owner's own savings, car or house can be used to settle business debts.

questions.question: In a partnership, the profits are usually _________ among the partners.
questions.expected: shared
questions.memo: Partners share the profits (and the losses), usually according to their partnership agreement.

questions.question: A sole trader's shop runs up large debts it cannot pay. Is the owner's house safe?
options: No — because of unlimited liability, personal property like the house can be taken
Yes — a sole trader has limited liability
Yes — the business is a separate legal person
No — but only the shop's stock can be taken
questions.expected: No — because of unlimited liability, personal property like the house can be taken
questions.memo: This is the common trap: a sole trader has UNLIMITED liability, so the owner's house and savings are at risk for business debts.

questions.question: What is a key advantage of a partnership over a sole trader?
options: More capital and a wider range of skills from several owners
The business becomes a separate legal person
Only one person makes all decisions
questions.expected: More capital and a wider range of skills from several owners
questions.memo: Partners bring more money and different skills than one person alone. (Liability is still unlimited, though.)

questions.question: Sort each feature by whether it describes a sole trader, a partnership, or both.

items.text: One owner keeps all the profit
Owned by two or more people
No separate legal identity from the owners

questions.expected: All six features sorted correctly (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Sole trader = one owner, all profit; partnership = several owners, shared profit. BOTH have unlimited liability and no separate legal identity.

questions.question: What usually happens to a sole trader's business when the owner dies?
options: It usually comes to an end, because it has no continuity
It carries on forever as a separate legal person
It automatically becomes a public company
questions.expected: It usually comes to an end, because it has no continuity
questions.memo: A sole trader has no continuity: the business is tied to the owner, so it usually ends when the owner dies or retires.

questions.question: Compare the two owners' descriptions, then decide which source each statement matches.

source_a.text: I run my tailoring shop on my own. I make every decision and keep all the profit, but I put in all the money myself, and if the shop owes money they can come after my own savings.

source_b.text: My sister and I own our catering business together. We share the start-up money and the profits and split the workload. But if one of us runs up a business debt, we are both responsible for paying it.

statements.text: The owner keeps all the profit alone.
The owners share the start-up money.
The owner(s) can be held personally responsible for the business's debts.
The business is a separate legal person that protects the owners' savings.

questions.expected: Match each statement: s1 a_only, s2 b_only, s3 both, s4 neither (≥75%)
questions.memo: Sole trader keeps all profit; the partnership shares the money. BOTH carry unlimited liability, and neither is a separate legal person — so personal savings are never fully protected.

questions.question: A sole trader's business income is taxed in the owner's _________ name.
questions.expected: personal
questions.memo: Because a sole trader is not a separate legal person, the profit is taxed as the owner's personal income.

questions.question: Which of these is a disadvantage of a partnership?
options: Each partner can be held responsible for another partner's business debts
There is too much capital available
Only one person can ever make decisions
questions.expected: Each partner can be held responsible for another partner's business debts
questions.memo: A disadvantage of a partnership is shared, unlimited liability — one partner's debt can fall on the others.

questions.question: True or false: A partnership has a separate legal identity from its partners.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — a partnership is not a separate legal person. The partners and the business are legally the same, which is why liability is unlimited.

questions.question: Which of these is a disadvantage of being a sole trader?
options: Limited capital and the whole workload falls on one person
All profit is shared with others
The owner has no control over decisions
questions.expected: Limited capital and the whole workload falls on one person
questions.memo: A sole trader is limited by the money and time of one person, and carries the whole burden alone — a real disadvantage.

questions.question: Sort each point as an advantage or a disadvantage of a sole trader.

items.text: No continuity if the owner dies

questions.expected: All six points sorted as advantage or disadvantage (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Advantages: all profit, easy to start, full control. Disadvantages: unlimited liability, limited capital, no continuity.

questions.question: Thandi wants full control of her small business and to keep all the profit, and she has only a little money to start. Which form best suits her, and why?
options: A sole trader, because it gives full control and all the profit and is easy to start
A partnership, because she wants to work alone
A sole trader, because it gives her limited liability
A partnership, because she wants to keep all the profit
questions.expected: A sole trader, because it gives full control and all the profit and is easy to start
questions.memo: Wanting full control, all the profit and an easy, cheap start points to a sole trader — though she must accept unlimited liability.

questions.question: Two friends pool their savings and skills to open a business together. Which statement best evaluates a partnership for them?
options: They gain more capital and shared skills, but must accept that they are both liable for the business's debts
They get limited liability and a separate legal person
They each keep all the profit for themselves
Neither of them is responsible for any debt
questions.expected: They gain more capital and shared skills, but must accept that they are both liable for the business's debts
questions.memo: A partnership brings more money and skills, but the trade-off is shared, unlimited liability — each partner can be held responsible for the debts.

questions.question: Why do both a sole trader and a partnership carry unlimited liability?
options: Because neither is a separate legal person, so the owners and the business are treated as one
Because both are owned by the government
Because both sell shares to the public
Because the law forces all businesses to have unlimited liability
questions.expected: Because neither is a separate legal person, so the owners and the business are treated as one
questions.memo: Neither form is a separate legal person, so in law the owners ARE the business — which is why their personal assets are at risk.

questions.question: Sort each statement by whether it is true of a sole trader only, a partnership only, or both.

items.text: Owned and run by one person
Owners are personally liable for debts
Owned by two or more people
Profits divided according to an agreement

questions.expected: All six statements sorted correctly (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: One owner and full control = sole trader; several owners and divided profit = partnership. Unlimited liability and no separate legal identity belong to BOTH.

BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A2.title: Forms of ownership: companies, CC & co-operatives
BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A2.description: The characteristics, advantages and disadvantages of the close corporation, non-profit company, profit companies (private, personal liability, public, state-owned) and co-operatives — focusing on legal personality, limited liability, capital and the rules on selling shares.
BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A2.strand: T2 — Socio-economic issues, social responsibility, entrepreneurship & ownership
BUS.G10.T2.OWNERSHIP.A2.recovery_strategy: A company is a separate legal person with limited liability. Private (Pty) Ltd cannot sell shares to the public; public (Ltd) can. No NEW close corporations can be registered (Companies Act 71 of 2008), but existing ones continue.

questions.question: A company is a separate _________ person, which means it can own property and be sued in its own name.
questions.expected: legal
questions.memo: A company is a separate legal person — in law it stands apart from its owners, so it can own things and be sued on its own.

questions.question: True or false: A public company (Ltd) can sell its shares to the general public.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A public company (Ltd) may offer its shares to the public, often by listing on the JSE.

questions.question: The letters (Pty) Ltd after a company's name show that it is a _________ company.
questions.expected: private
questions.memo: (Pty) Ltd means a private company — its shares are not offered to the public.

questions.question: What does limited liability mean for the owners of a company?
options: They can only lose the money they invested, not their personal belongings
They are personally responsible for all the company's debts
They must sell their houses if the company fails
questions.expected: They can only lose the money they invested, not their personal belongings
questions.memo: Limited liability protects owners: the most they can lose is what they put in, because the company is a separate legal person.

questions.question: True or false: A private company (Pty) Ltd can sell its shares to the general public.
questions.expected: False
questions.memo: False — this is a common mistake. A private (Pty) Ltd company may NOT offer shares to the public; only a public (Ltd) company can.

questions.question: A company that does not aim to make a profit, such as a charity, is called a _________ company.
questions.expected: non-profit
questions.memo: A non-profit company (NPC) is set up for a public benefit or social cause, not to make profit for owners.

questions.question: A private company (Pty) Ltd wants to list and sell shares on the JSE. What must happen first?
options: It must first convert into a public company, because private companies cannot sell shares to the public
Nothing — a private company can already list on the JSE
It must first become a sole trader
It must first become a close corporation
questions.expected: It must first convert into a public company, because private companies cannot sell shares to the public
questions.memo: Private companies cannot offer shares to the public. To raise money on the JSE it must first become a public (Ltd) company.

questions.question: Which of these is an advantage of forming a company rather than being a sole trader?
options: Limited liability and continuity that protect the owners and the business
The business ends as soon as one owner leaves
Profits are taxed in the owner's personal name
questions.expected: Limited liability and continuity that protect the owners and the business
questions.memo: A company offers limited liability and continuity — it survives changes of owner and protects personal assets.

questions.question: Sort each feature by whether it describes a private company or a public company.

items.text: Shares may not be sold to the public
Can list its shares on the JSE
Usually a smaller, closely held business
Can raise large capital from the public

questions.expected: All six features sorted private vs public (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Private (Pty) Ltd: no public shares, smaller, closely held. Public (Ltd): can list and raise capital from the public.

questions.question: What does it mean that a company has 'separate legal personality'?
options: The company can own property, sign contracts and be sued in its own name, apart from its owners
The owners and the company are legally the same person
Only the directors can be sued, never the company
questions.expected: The company can own property, sign contracts and be sued in its own name, apart from its owners
questions.memo: Separate legal personality means the company is its own 'person' in law — it owns, contracts and is sued in its own name.

questions.question: Since the Companies Act of 2008, no NEW _________ may be registered, although existing ones continue.
questions.expected: close corporations
questions.memo: No new close corporations (CCs) can be registered since the 2008 Act, but those already registered keep operating.

questions.question: What is a co-operative?
options: A business owned and run by its members for their mutual benefit
A business owned by the government only
A company that sells shares on the JSE
A business owned by a single person
questions.expected: A business owned and run by its members for their mutual benefit
questions.memo: A co-operative is owned and controlled by its members, who share in the benefits and profits according to their use of it.

questions.question: Sort each form of ownership by whether it has limited or unlimited liability.
questions.expected: All six forms sorted by liability type (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Companies and CCs are separate legal persons, so they have limited liability. Sole traders and partnerships are not, so liability is unlimited.

questions.question: True or false: A company has continuity, so it can carry on even if an owner sells out or dies.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Because a company is a separate legal person, it has continuity — it keeps going regardless of who the owners are.

questions.question: What is a state-owned company (SOC)?
options: A company owned by the government that provides goods or services to the public
A company owned only by its workers
questions.expected: A company owned by the government that provides goods or services to the public
questions.memo: A state-owned company is owned by government (for example Eskom or Transnet) and supplies key goods or services.

questions.question: What is the main difference between a private and a public company?
options: A public company may offer shares to the public; a private company may not
A private company has more shareholders than a public one
A public company is always smaller
A private company is owned by the state
questions.expected: A public company may offer shares to the public; a private company may not
questions.memo: The key difference is selling shares: public companies can offer shares to the public, private companies cannot.

questions.question: A business needs to raise a very large amount of capital by inviting thousands of investors to buy shares. Which form best suits it, and why?
options: A public company, because only it can offer shares to the public and raise large capital
A private company, because it can list on the JSE
A sole trader, because one owner can raise the most money
A partnership, because partners have limited liability
questions.expected: A public company, because only it can offer shares to the public and raise large capital
questions.memo: Raising big money from many public investors needs a public company — the only form allowed to sell shares to the public.

questions.question: Why does a company's limited liability protect its owners in a way a sole trader's does not?
options: Because the company is a separate legal person, owners risk only their investment, not their personal assets
Because owners of a company never make any decisions
Because a company can never have debts
Because the government pays a company's debts
questions.expected: Because the company is a separate legal person, owners risk only their investment, not their personal assets
questions.memo: Limited liability flows from separate legal personality: the company owes the debt, not the owners, so their personal assets are safe.

questions.question: The owner of a growing CC asks to register a brand-new close corporation for a second venture. How should this be answered?
options: No new CCs can be registered since the 2008 Act, though her existing CC may continue; she could form a company instead
She can easily register as many new CCs as she likes
CCs were never allowed in South Africa
Her existing CC must be closed immediately
questions.expected: No new CCs can be registered since the 2008 Act, though her existing CC may continue; she could form a company instead
questions.memo: Since the Companies Act of 2008, no new CCs may be registered. Existing CCs carry on, but for a new venture she would register a company.

questions.question: Match each statement to the form of ownership it describes.

items.text: Shares held by a small group, not the public
Lists its shares on the stock exchange
Owned by members for their mutual benefit
May invite the public to buy shares
Profits shared among the members who use it

questions.expected: All six statements matched to the correct form (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Private = closely held, no public shares, (Pty) Ltd. Public = lists and sells shares to the public. Co-operative = owned by members who share the benefit.

BUS.G10.T3.CREATIVE.A1.title: Creative thinking & problem-solving
BUS.G10.T3.CREATIVE.A1.description: How creative thinking supports sustainable business; the problem-solving cycle; the difference between problem-solving and decision-making; and creative-thinking techniques (brainstorming, mind-mapping, Delphi, Nominal Group, Force-Field Analysis, Forced Combinations).
BUS.G10.T3.CREATIVE.A1.strand: T3 — Creative thinking, opportunity, location, contracts, presentation & the business plan
BUS.G10.T3.CREATIVE.A1.recovery_strategy: Problem-solving is the full cycle of fixing a problem; decision-making is one step inside it (choosing an option). Creative-thinking techniques (brainstorming, mind-maps) generate the options.

questions.question: What is creative thinking in business?
options: Coming up with new and useful ideas to solve problems or improve the business
Copying exactly what every competitor does
questions.expected: Coming up with new and useful ideas to solve problems or improve the business
questions.memo: Creative thinking means generating fresh, useful ideas — to solve problems, find opportunities and keep the business growing.

questions.question: Problem-solving is best described as _________.
options: the whole process of finding and applying a solution to a problem
questions.expected: the whole process of finding and applying a solution to a problem
questions.memo: Problem-solving is the full process of working through a problem to a solution. Decision-making is just one step inside it.

questions.question: Decision-making is best described as _________.
options: choosing the best option from the choices available
questions.expected: choosing the best option from the choices available
questions.memo: Decision-making is choosing between options. It is one step within the larger problem-solving process.

questions.question: True or false: Brainstorming is a technique used to generate many ideas quickly.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Brainstorming gathers many ideas quickly without judging them at first — a popular creative-thinking technique.

questions.question: A diagram that branches out from a central idea to show related thoughts is called a _________.
questions.expected: mind-map
questions.memo: A mind-map starts with a central idea and branches out to related ideas — a creative-thinking tool for organising thoughts.

questions.question: True or false: Creative thinking can help a business stay sustainable by finding better ways to work.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Creative thinking helps a business adapt, cut waste and find new opportunities — all of which support long-term sustainability.

questions.question: Put the problem-solving steps in the correct order.

items.text: Choose and implement the best solution

questions.expected: identify, define, generate, choose, evaluate
questions.memo: First spot the problem, then understand it, generate options, choose and act, and finally check the result. Choosing is just one step in this cycle.

questions.question: Why is decision-making described as a 'part' of problem-solving?
options: Choosing the best option is one step within the full problem-solving cycle
They are unrelated to each other
questions.expected: Choosing the best option is one step within the full problem-solving cycle
questions.memo: Problem-solving includes generating options AND choosing one. Decision-making is that choosing step, sitting inside the bigger cycle.

questions.question: Sort each item as a creative-thinking TECHNIQUE or NOT a technique.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Brainstorming, mind-mapping, Delphi and Force-Field Analysis are creative-thinking techniques. Paying bills and filing tax are routine tasks, not techniques.

questions.question: In the Delphi technique, ideas and opinions are gathered from experts by _________.
options: asking them separately, often in rounds, and combining their answers
forcing everyone to shout at once
letting only the manager decide alone
questions.expected: asking them separately, often in rounds, and combining their answers
questions.memo: The Delphi technique collects experts' views separately over several rounds, then combines them — useful when you want unbiased expert input.

questions.question: A team weighs the forces pushing FOR a change against the forces pushing AGAINST it. Which technique is this?
questions.expected: Force-Field Analysis
questions.memo: Force-Field Analysis lists the forces for and against a change to decide whether to go ahead — weighing the push and the resistance.

questions.question: True or false: Creative-thinking techniques are mainly used to GENERATE possible solutions, which the team then decides between.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Techniques like brainstorming and mind-mapping generate options; the team then makes a decision by choosing the best one.

questions.question: A shop owner notices sales are dropping. What is the FIRST step of problem-solving she should take?
options: Identify and clearly define what the problem actually is
Evaluate a solution before trying anything
questions.expected: Identify and clearly define what the problem actually is
questions.memo: Problem-solving starts by identifying and defining the real problem. Jumping straight to a solution risks fixing the wrong thing.

questions.question: The Nominal Group technique helps a team by _________.
options: letting each member write ideas first, then sharing and ranking them together
letting the loudest person decide everything
questions.expected: letting each member write ideas first, then sharing and ranking them together
questions.memo: The Nominal Group technique has members write ideas privately first, then share and rank them — so quieter members' ideas count too.

questions.question: Sort each action as part of GENERATING ideas or part of DECIDING.

items.text: Choosing the single best solution to use
Picking which option to put into action
Listing every idea without judging it yet
Selecting the option with the best results

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Generating spreads out many ideas (brainstorm, mind-map, list); deciding narrows down to the one best choice.

questions.question: Why is it risky to make a decision before generating several options?
options: The team may miss a better solution it never considered
It always saves the most money
questions.expected: The team may miss a better solution it never considered
questions.memo: Deciding too early, before generating options, risks settling for a weak solution and missing a better idea.

questions.question: A learner says: 'Problem-solving and decision-making are exactly the same thing.' Which response is correct?
options: No — problem-solving is the whole cycle; decision-making is just the choosing step inside it
Yes, they are identical in every way
No — decision-making includes problem-solving as one step
questions.expected: No — problem-solving is the whole cycle; decision-making is just the choosing step inside it
questions.memo: They are related but not the same. Problem-solving is the full process; decision-making is the single step of choosing within it.

questions.question: Why does combining a creative-thinking technique with the problem-solving cycle work well?
options: The technique generates many options, and the cycle guides choosing and applying the best one
The technique replaces the need to act at all
The cycle stops any new ideas
questions.expected: The technique generates many options, and the cycle guides choosing and applying the best one
questions.memo: Creative techniques fill the 'generate options' step with rich ideas, while the cycle ensures the best one is chosen, applied and reviewed.

questions.question: A business tries one solution but the problem returns. Which step of the cycle should have warned them, and why?
options: Monitoring and evaluating, because it checks whether the solution actually worked
Identifying the problem, because that ends the cycle
Generating ideas, because that is the last step
None — the cycle has no checking step
questions.expected: Monitoring and evaluating, because it checks whether the solution actually worked
questions.memo: The monitor-and-evaluate step checks if the solution worked. Skipping it lets a returning problem go unnoticed until it is serious.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about creative thinking and problem-solving.

items.text: Problem-solving is the full cycle of fixing a problem
Decision-making is the same as the whole cycle
Creative thinking means never changing anything
Evaluating checks whether the solution worked
You should always decide before understanding the problem

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Problem-solving is the whole cycle; deciding is one step in it; techniques generate ideas; and you must understand a problem before solving it.

BUS.G10.T3.OPPORTUNITY.A1.title: Business opportunity, research & SWOT
BUS.G10.T3.OPPORTUNITY.A1.description: Spotting a business opportunity from researched needs; research instruments (questionnaires, interviews) and research ethics; and using a SWOT analysis correctly — Strengths and Weaknesses are internal, Opportunities and Threats are external.
BUS.G10.T3.OPPORTUNITY.A1.strand: T3 — Creative thinking, opportunity, location, contracts, presentation & the business plan
BUS.G10.T3.OPPORTUNITY.A1.recovery_strategy: SWOT: Strengths & Weaknesses are INTERNAL (inside the business); Opportunities & Threats are EXTERNAL (outside). Strengths/Opportunities help; Weaknesses/Threats harm.

questions.question: What does SWOT stand for?
questions.expected: Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities, Threats
questions.memo: SWOT stands for Strengths, Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats — a tool for checking if a venture is viable.

questions.question: True or false: Strengths and weaknesses are internal to the business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Strengths and weaknesses are internal — they are things inside the business that it can control.

questions.question: A _________ is a set of written questions used to collect information from many people.
questions.expected: questionnaire
questions.memo: A questionnaire is a research instrument — a list of set questions used to gather information from many respondents.

questions.question: Which of these is an EXTERNAL factor in a SWOT analysis?
questions.expected: A threat
questions.memo: Opportunities and threats are external (outside the business). Strengths and weaknesses are internal.

questions.question: True or false: Opportunities and threats come from outside the business.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Opportunities and threats are external — they come from the market and macro environments outside the business.

questions.question: A business _________ is a gap or unmet need in the market that a business could fill.
questions.expected: opportunity
questions.memo: A business opportunity is an unmet need or gap in the market that the business can turn into a venture.

questions.question: A strong new competitor opens nearby. In a SWOT analysis this should be listed as a:
questions.expected: Threat
questions.memo: A competitor comes from OUTSIDE and could harm the business, so it is a threat — not a weakness (which is internal).

questions.question: The business has a skilled, motivated team. In a SWOT analysis this is a:
questions.expected: Strength
questions.memo: Skilled staff are inside the business and help it, so they are an internal strength.

questions.question: Sort each SWOT factor as internal or external.

items.text: The skills of the business's staff
A new law affecting the industry
A new competitor entering the market

questions.expected: All six factors sorted internal vs external (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Internal = things inside the business (staff, cash, equipment). External = things outside it (laws, demand, competitors).

questions.question: Demand for the business's type of product is growing fast. In a SWOT analysis this is a:
questions.expected: Opportunity
questions.memo: Growing demand comes from OUTSIDE and helps the business, so it is an opportunity.

questions.question: Strengths and weaknesses are _________ factors that the business can control.
questions.expected: internal
questions.memo: Strengths and weaknesses are internal — inside the business and within its control.

questions.question: Sort each SWOT factor by whether it helps or harms the business.
questions.expected: All six factors sorted helps vs harms (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Strengths and opportunities help the business; weaknesses and threats harm it. SWOT sorts factors by both helps/harms and internal/external.

questions.question: Which research instrument is best for getting detailed, in-depth opinions from one person face to face?
options: A printed questionnaire posted to thousands
questions.expected: An interview
questions.memo: An interview lets the researcher ask follow-up questions and get detailed, in-depth answers from a person.

questions.question: True or false: A weakness is an internal factor that holds the business back.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A weakness is internal and harms the business — something inside it that limits performance.

questions.question: Which of these is good research ethics (protocol) when collecting information from people?
options: Getting their consent, keeping their answers private and being honest about the purpose
Making up answers to save time
Sharing people's names and answers publicly
questions.expected: Getting their consent, keeping their answers private and being honest about the purpose
questions.memo: Ethical research means asking permission, protecting people's privacy and being honest about why you are collecting the information.

questions.question: The business's machines are old and break down often. In a SWOT analysis this is a:
questions.expected: Weakness
questions.memo: Old machines are INSIDE the business and hold it back, so they are an internal weakness — not an external threat.

questions.question: Loyal customers who keep coming back belong in which part of a SWOT analysis?
options: Strength, because it is an internal advantage that helps the business
Threat, because customers are outside the business
questions.expected: Strength, because it is an internal advantage that helps the business
questions.memo: A base of loyal customers is an internal advantage the business has built, so it is a strength.

questions.question: Why should an entrepreneur do research and a SWOT analysis BEFORE starting a venture?
options: To check there is a real need and to weigh the venture's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
To avoid ever having to make a decision
Because the law forces every business to do a SWOT
To copy a competitor's exact business plan
questions.expected: To check there is a real need and to weigh the venture's strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats
questions.memo: Research confirms a real market need, and a SWOT weighs the venture's internal and external position — together they show whether it is viable.

questions.question: The owner has very little business experience. Where does this belong in a SWOT analysis, and why?
options: A weakness, because it is an internal factor that holds the business back
A threat, because experience comes from outside
A strength, because new owners try harder
An opportunity, because it is external
questions.expected: A weakness, because it is an internal factor that holds the business back
questions.memo: The owner's lack of experience is internal and limits the business, so it is a weakness — not an external threat.

questions.question: Sort each factor into the correct SWOT category.

items.text: Rising raw-material prices across the industry

questions.expected: All six factors in the correct SWOT category (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Internal helps = strength (trusted brand, skilled managers); internal harms = weakness (staff turnover, old systems); external harms = threat (competitor, rising industry prices).

BUS.G10.T3.LOCATION.A1.title: Business location factors
BUS.G10.T3.LOCATION.A1.description: Factors that affect where a business should locate — raw materials, the potential market, transport, infrastructure, labour, the cost of electricity and water, climate, regulations and crime — and matching the most important factor to the type of business.
BUS.G10.T3.LOCATION.A1.strand: T3 — Creative thinking, opportunity, location, contracts, presentation & the business plan
BUS.G10.T3.LOCATION.A1.recovery_strategy: Match the factor to the business: raw-material businesses locate near materials; service businesses locate near customers; factories weigh transport and labour costs.

questions.question: Why does WHERE a business is located matter?
options: The right location can lower costs and bring in more customers
Only the product matters, not where it is sold
Location only matters to the government
questions.expected: The right location can lower costs and bring in more customers
questions.memo: A good location can cut costs (transport, materials) and attract customers, so choosing it carefully is an important decision.

questions.question: A business that needs heavy raw materials, like a mine, should locate _________.
questions.expected: near the raw materials
questions.memo: Heavy raw-material businesses locate near the materials to cut the high cost of transporting them.

questions.question: A small shop or service business usually does best when located _________.
options: where no one can find it
questions.expected: close to its customers
questions.memo: Shops and services depend on foot traffic, so they locate close to their customers — where people can easily reach them.

questions.question: True or false: Good roads, electricity and water supply (infrastructure) affect a business's location choice.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Infrastructure — roads, electricity, water — is a key location factor. Poor infrastructure raises costs and causes delays.

questions.question: The availability of workers with the right skills in an area is called the _________.
questions.expected: labour market
questions.memo: The labour market is the supply of workers and their skills in an area — an important factor when a business needs many or skilled employees.

questions.question: True or false: High crime in an area can raise a business's security costs and affect its location choice.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Crime is a location factor — a high-crime area means higher security costs and risk, which can push a business to locate elsewhere.

questions.question: Match each business to the location factor that matters MOST to it.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Match the factor to the business: material-processors locate near materials, services near customers, and delivery businesses near good transport.

questions.question: Why should a fruit-canning factory locate near the orchards?
options: Fresh fruit is bulky and spoils, so locating near it cuts transport cost and waste
It is the cheapest place to advertise
Fruit lasts forever, so location does not matter
questions.expected: Fresh fruit is bulky and spoils, so locating near it cuts transport cost and waste
questions.memo: Bulky, perishable raw materials like fresh fruit are expensive to move and spoil quickly, so the factory locates near the orchards.

questions.question: Why does a clothing shop choose a busy shopping centre rather than an industrial area?
options: It needs to be where many customers pass by
It needs to be near coal mines
Customers do not matter to a shop
questions.expected: It needs to be where many customers pass by
questions.memo: A shop relies on passing customers, so it locates in a busy centre rather than an industrial area with few shoppers.

questions.question: High electricity and water costs in an area mainly affect which kind of business most?
options: A factory that uses a lot of power and water
A business that uses no power at all
A purely online business with no premises
questions.expected: A factory that uses a lot of power and water
questions.memo: A factory uses large amounts of power and water, so the cost of these is a major location factor for it.

questions.question: Local regulations and taxes set by a municipality are a _________ factor in choosing a location.
questions.expected: legal/government
questions.memo: Municipal regulations and taxes are legal/government location factors — they affect what a business may do and what it must pay in an area.

questions.question: True or false: Climate can be a location factor for some businesses, such as farming or tourism.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Climate matters for businesses like farming (crops need the right weather) and tourism (visitors prefer good weather).

questions.question: A learner says: 'A coal mine should be located in the city centre near its customers.' Why is this wrong?
options: A mine must be located where the coal is found, not near customers
Correct — mines belong in city centres
questions.expected: A mine must be located where the coal is found, not near customers
questions.memo: A mine has no choice — it must be where the coal is. Locating near customers would be impossible and pointless.

questions.question: Sort each item as a location FACTOR or NOT a location factor.

items.text: The colour of the owner's car
Level of crime in the area

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Real location factors affect cost, access and risk (labour, materials, transport, crime). Personal trivia like a favourite show is not a location factor.

questions.question: Why might a business choose a location with a strong labour market?
options: It can more easily find the skilled workers it needs
questions.expected: It can more easily find the skilled workers it needs
questions.memo: A strong labour market means plenty of skilled workers available, making it easier and often cheaper for the business to hire.

questions.question: A delivery business depends most on which location factor?
questions.expected: Good transport routes and infrastructure
questions.memo: A delivery business lives on moving goods quickly, so good roads and transport links are its most important location factor.

questions.question: Two businesses both want to cut costs. A steel mill (heavy materials) and a hair salon (local service) should locate very differently. Why?
options: The mill saves most by being near its materials; the salon saves by being near its customers
Both should be in the same remote place
Both should locate near a coal mine
questions.expected: The mill saves most by being near its materials; the salon saves by being near its customers
questions.memo: The key factor depends on the business: a mill cuts cost by being near heavy materials, while a salon needs to be near the customers it serves.

questions.question: Why can a cheap location sometimes turn out to be a costly mistake?
options: If it is far from customers, materials or good transport, the savings can be wiped out by other costs
Cheap locations are always the best choice
Location never has any hidden costs
questions.expected: If it is far from customers, materials or good transport, the savings can be wiped out by other costs
questions.memo: A low rent can be a false saving if the location is far from customers, materials or transport — those extra costs and lost sales can outweigh it.

questions.question: An entrepreneur opening a busy takeaway weighs up several areas. Which combination of factors matters MOST?
options: Plenty of passing customers, good access and reasonable rent
Nearness to a coal mine and a cold climate
Distance from all people and roads
Only the colour of the building
questions.expected: Plenty of passing customers, good access and reasonable rent
questions.memo: A takeaway needs hungry customers passing by, easy access and affordable rent — the customer-facing factors matter most for a food service.

questions.question: Sort each statement as TRUE or FALSE about business location.

items.text: A shop usually locates near its customers
A mine should locate near its customers, not the ore
Crime can raise a business's security costs
Infrastructure has no effect on location
A heavy-material factory locates near its raw materials
The most important location factor is the same for every business

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: The best location depends on the business: shops go near customers, mines near the ore, factories near materials. Factors like crime and infrastructure always matter.

BUS.G10.T3.CONTRACTS.A1.title: Contracts & legal implications
BUS.G10.T3.CONTRACTS.A1.description: The definition of a contract and the business contracts of employment, insurance, lease, hire-purchase and rental — with the two parties to each and their rights and responsibilities.
BUS.G10.T3.CONTRACTS.A1.strand: T3 — Creative thinking, opportunity, location, contracts, presentation & the business plan
BUS.G10.T3.CONTRACTS.A1.recovery_strategy: Learn the pair for each contract: employment = employer/employee; insurance = insurer/insured; lease = lessor/lessee; hire-purchase = seller/buyer; rental = landlord/tenant.

questions.question: What is a contract?
options: A legal agreement between two or more parties that can be enforced by law
A friendly promise with no rules
questions.expected: A legal agreement between two or more parties that can be enforced by law
questions.memo: A contract is a legally binding agreement between parties. If one side breaks it, the law can enforce the agreement.

questions.question: The two parties to an employment contract are the employer and the _________.
questions.expected: employee
questions.memo: An employment contract is between the employer (who gives the job) and the employee (who does the work).

questions.question: An agreement to rent a building for business use over a long period is a _________.
questions.expected: lease
questions.memo: A lease is a contract to use property (like a building) for a period in return for payment, between the lessor and the lessee.

questions.question: True or false: An insurance contract is between the insurer and the insured.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: An insurance contract is between the insurer (the company that covers the risk) and the insured (who pays premiums for cover).

questions.question: Buying goods now and paying them off in instalments, with the seller keeping ownership until the last payment, is a _________ agreement.
questions.expected: hire-purchase
questions.memo: Hire-purchase lets a buyer pay in instalments while the seller keeps ownership until the final payment is made.

questions.question: True or false: The two parties to a rental agreement are the landlord and the tenant.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A rental agreement is between the landlord (who owns the property) and the tenant (who pays to use it).

questions.question: Match each contract to its correct pair of parties.

items.text: A worker and the business that hired them
A company covering a risk and the policyholder
The owner of premises and the one who leases them

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Employment = employer/employee; insurance = insurer/insured; lease = lessor/lessee. Learn each contract's pair.

questions.question: In an employment contract, what is a key responsibility of the EMPLOYER?
options: To pay the agreed wage and provide a safe workplace
To do the employee's work for them
questions.expected: To pay the agreed wage and provide a safe workplace
questions.memo: The employer must pay the agreed wage and provide safe working conditions; the employee must do the agreed work properly.

questions.question: In an insurance contract, what is the main responsibility of the INSURED?
options: To pay the agreed premiums on time
To pay out claims to others
questions.expected: To pay the agreed premiums on time
questions.memo: The insured pays premiums; in return the insurer pays out if the insured event (like theft or fire) happens.

questions.question: A learner says: 'The parties to a lease are the insurer and the insured.' What is the mistake?
options: A lease is between the lessor and the lessee, not the insurer and insured
A lease has only one party
A lease is between employer and employee
questions.expected: A lease is between the lessor and the lessee, not the insurer and insured
questions.memo: Insurer and insured belong to an insurance contract. A lease is between the lessor (owner) and the lessee (user).

questions.question: In a hire-purchase agreement, who owns the goods until the final instalment is paid?
questions.expected: The seller
questions.memo: Under hire-purchase the seller keeps ownership until the buyer makes the last payment, even though the buyer uses the goods in the meantime.

questions.question: True or false: A contract must be agreed to freely by all parties, without force.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A valid contract requires free agreement by all parties. An agreement forced on someone is not a proper contract.

questions.question: Match each pair of parties to the correct contract.

items.text: A shop selling on instalments and its customer
A property owner and the person renting
A business and the worker it pays

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Hire-purchase = seller/buyer; rental = landlord/tenant; employment = employer/employee. Each contract has its own pair.

questions.question: Why is it important that a business contract is in writing?
options: It records what each party agreed, so it can be proved and enforced if there is a dispute
It hides the agreement from the parties
questions.expected: It records what each party agreed, so it can be proved and enforced if there is a dispute
questions.memo: A written contract is clear proof of what was agreed, which makes it far easier to enforce if a disagreement arises.

questions.question: A tenant rents a shop and stops paying rent. Which party has the right to act, and under which contract?
options: The landlord, under the rental agreement
The insurer, under the insurance contract
The employee, under the employment contract
questions.expected: The landlord, under the rental agreement
questions.memo: Unpaid rent is a breach of the rental agreement, so the landlord has the right to act against the tenant.

questions.question: Which situation correctly matches the contract to its purpose?
options: Insurance protects against losses like fire or theft for an agreed premium
Employment is used to insure a car
A lease is used to pay salaries
Hire-purchase is used to rent out a house
questions.expected: Insurance protects against losses like fire or theft for an agreed premium
questions.memo: Each contract has its job: insurance covers risks for a premium; employment hires staff; a lease/rental provides premises; hire-purchase buys goods over time.

questions.question: Why does knowing the correct parties to each contract matter for a business?
options: It shows who has which rights and responsibilities if a dispute arises
It is only useful for passing a test
The parties never matter in practice
It lets the business avoid all contracts
questions.expected: It shows who has which rights and responsibilities if a dispute arises
questions.memo: Knowing the parties tells you who owes what and who can claim what, which is essential when something goes wrong.

questions.question: A business takes goods on hire-purchase and misses several payments. Why can the seller usually take the goods back?
options: The seller still owns the goods until the final instalment is paid
The buyer never had to pay anything
The goods belong to the insurer
questions.expected: The seller still owns the goods until the final instalment is paid
questions.memo: Because ownership stays with the seller until the last payment, the seller can reclaim the goods if the buyer defaults.

questions.question: A factory burns down. The business claims from its cover. Which contract and party let it recover its loss?
options: The insurance contract — the insurer pays the insured for the covered loss
The lease — the lessee pays the lessor
The employment contract — the employer pays the employee
Hire-purchase — the buyer pays the seller
questions.expected: The insurance contract — the insurer pays the insured for the covered loss
questions.memo: Insurance exists for exactly this: after a covered loss like fire, the insurer pays out to the insured business.

questions.question: Match each contract to its correct pair of parties.

items.text: The policyholder and the company covering the risk
The owner of premises and the long-term user
The property owner and the short-term renter

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Insurance = insurer/insured; lease = lessor/lessee; rental = landlord/tenant. Matching the right pair to the right contract is the key skill.

BUS.G10.T3.PRESENT.A1.title: Presentation of information
BUS.G10.T3.PRESENT.A1.description: Presenting business information clearly: the difference between verbal and non-verbal formats, using reports with tables, graphs and diagrams, supporting a verbal presentation with visual aids, and designing a clear layout.
BUS.G10.T3.PRESENT.A1.strand: T3 — Creative thinking, opportunity, location, contracts, presentation & the business plan
BUS.G10.T3.PRESENT.A1.recovery_strategy: Verbal = spoken/words (a talk, a report's text). Non-verbal = visuals (tables, graphs, diagrams, pictures). Good presentations put the most important information first and keep visuals clear.

questions.question: A 'verbal' presentation uses mainly _________.
questions.expected: spoken or written words
questions.memo: Verbal means words — spoken (a talk) or written (a report's text). Non-verbal means visuals like graphs and pictures.

questions.question: Which of these is a NON-VERBAL way of presenting information?
questions.expected: A bar graph
questions.memo: A bar graph is a visual, so it is non-verbal. Speeches, paragraphs and phone calls all use words, so they are verbal.

questions.question: True or false: A table of figures is a non-verbal way of presenting information.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: A table presents information visually in rows and columns, so it is non-verbal — like graphs and diagrams.

questions.question: Slides, charts and handouts used during a talk are called _________.
questions.expected: visual aids
questions.memo: Visual aids — slides, charts, handouts — support a spoken presentation and help the audience follow and remember it.

questions.question: True or false: A good presentation puts the most important information first.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Leading with the most important information grabs attention and makes sure the key message gets across, even if time runs short.

questions.question: A written report that explains the business's results in sentences and paragraphs is mainly a _________ presentation.
questions.expected: verbal
questions.memo: Sentences and paragraphs are words, so a written report's text is a verbal presentation (even though it may include some visuals).

questions.question: Sort each format as VERBAL or NON-VERBAL.

items.text: A spoken speech to the team

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: If it uses words (spoken or written), it is verbal. If it shows information as a picture, chart, diagram or table, it is non-verbal.

questions.question: Why might a presenter use a graph instead of a long list of numbers?
options: A graph shows the pattern at a glance and is easier to understand
Numbers can never be shown visually
A graph always confuses the audience
questions.expected: A graph shows the pattern at a glance and is easier to understand
questions.memo: A graph turns numbers into a picture, so the audience can see trends and comparisons quickly instead of reading a long list.

questions.question: A learner says: 'A bar graph is a verbal presentation because it has a few words on it.' What is the mistake?
options: A bar graph mainly shows information visually, so it is non-verbal
questions.expected: A bar graph mainly shows information visually, so it is non-verbal
questions.memo: A few labels do not make a graph verbal. Its main job is to show information as a picture, so it is non-verbal.

questions.question: Put the steps of preparing a presentation in a sensible order.

items.text: Decide the purpose and who the audience is
Design the layout and choose visual aids
Get feedback and improve next time

questions.expected: audience, gather, design, deliver, feedback
questions.memo: Know your purpose and audience first, gather and organise the content, design clear visuals, deliver, then learn from feedback.

questions.question: Which is a feature of a clear, well-designed presentation layout?
options: Headings, short points and easy-to-read visuals
Tiny print packed edge to edge
As many words as possible on each slide
questions.expected: Headings, short points and easy-to-read visuals
questions.memo: A clear layout uses headings, short points and readable visuals so the audience can follow it easily.

questions.question: True or false: Visual aids should support the spoken words, not replace the whole presentation.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Visual aids back up what the presenter says; they should not be so crowded that they replace the explanation.

questions.question: Sort each item as a VISUAL AID or NOT a visual aid for a presentation.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Visual aids help present information (slides, handouts, charts, diagrams). Unrelated objects like lunch or keys are not visual aids.

questions.question: Why should information in a report be accurate and succinct (short and to the point)?
options: So readers get correct information quickly without wading through extra words
So the report is as long as possible
So the figures can be wrong
So no one can understand it
questions.expected: So readers get correct information quickly without wading through extra words
questions.memo: Accurate, succinct information respects the reader's time and avoids mistakes, so the message lands clearly and quickly.

questions.question: Which presentation choice best suits comparing sales across four years?
options: A graph, because it shows the trend over time clearly
A long spoken list of every number
A single sentence with no figures
questions.expected: A graph, because it shows the trend over time clearly
questions.memo: Comparing values over time is exactly what a graph does well — the audience sees the trend at a glance.

questions.question: True or false: Knowing the audience helps a presenter choose the right words and visuals.
questions.expected: True
questions.memo: Understanding the audience lets the presenter pitch the language and visuals at the right level so the message is understood.

questions.question: A presenter crams tiny text and ten graphs onto one slide and reads every word aloud. Which evaluation is best?
options: The layout is poor; clear slides with key points and readable visuals would communicate better
The slide is perfect because it has lots of information
More text always means a better presentation
questions.expected: The layout is poor; clear slides with key points and readable visuals would communicate better
